IBNATIYYA-FULL:v4p461/r7.anchor: وإنما منعه الله تعالى من الشعر ترفيعا له عما في قول الشعراء من التخييل، وتزويق القول

IBNATIYYA-FULL:v4p461/r8.author: Ibn ʿAṭiyya
IBNATIYYA-FULL:v4p461/r8.speaker: author
IBNATIYYA-FULL:v4p461/r8.claim: The pronoun in ʿallamnāhu refers unanimously to Muḥammad.
IBNATIYYA-FULL:v4p461/r8.anchor: والضمير في علمناه عائد على محمد صلى الله عليه وسلم قولا واحدا

IBNATIYYA-FULL:v4p461/r9.author: Ibn ʿAṭiyya
IBNATIYYA-FULL:v4p461/r9.speaker: author
IBNATIYYA-FULL:v4p461/r9.claim: The pronoun in lahu may refer either to Muḥammad or to the Qur'an, which is supplied by proximity despite not being named.
IBNATIYYA-FULL:v4p461/r9.anchor: والضمير في له يحتمل أن يعود على محمد ويحتمل أن يعود على القرآن

BURSEVI:v7p335#2/r1.author: İsmāʿīl Ḥaqqī Bursevī
BURSEVI:v7p335#2/r1.speaker: author
BURSEVI:v7p335#2/r1.claim: The verse refutes the charge that Muhammad was a poet; denying that God taught him poetry implies more forcefully that he was not a poet and the Quran is not poetry.
BURSEVI:v7p335#2/r1.anchor: رد وإبطال لما كانوا يقولون في حقه عليه السلام من أنه شاعر وما يقوله شعر

BURSEVI:v7p335#2/r2.author: İsmāʿīl Ḥaqqī Bursevī
BURSEVI:v7p335#2/r2.speaker: الراغب
BURSEVI:v7p335#2/r2.claim: Al-Raghib traces shiʿr to fine, precise knowing and says a poet was so named for acuity and subtle knowledge; common usage later meant metered, rhymed speech.
BURSEVI:v7p335#2/r2.anchor: قال الراغب : يقال : شعرت أصبت الشعر

BURSEVI:v7p335#2/r3.author: İsmāʿīl Ḥaqqī Bursevī
BURSEVI:v7p335#2/r3.speaker: القاموس
BURSEVI:v7p335#2/r3.claim: Al-Qamus says poetry came to denote metered verse because of its prestige, although all knowledge may be called poetry; it gives the plural ashʿār and related senses of knowing and discerning.
BURSEVI:v7p335#2/r3.anchor: في "القاموس" : الشعر غلب على منظوم القول لشرفه

BURSEVI:v7p335#2/r4.author: İsmāʿīl Ḥaqqī Bursevī
BURSEVI:v7p335#2/r4.speaker: الحكماء القدماء
BURSEVI:v7p335#2/r4.claim: Ancient philosophers define poetry by imaginative premises, not meter or rhyme; meter and rhyme can assist imagination, and premises may combine poetic, persuasive, or demonstrative elements.
BURSEVI:v7p335#2/r4.anchor: والشعر عند الحكماء القدماء ليس على وزن وقافية ولا الوزن والقافية ركن في الشعر عندهم

BURSEVI:v7p335#2/r5.author: İsmāʿīl Ḥaqqī Bursevī
BURSEVI:v7p335#2/r5.speaker: بعضهم
BURSEVI:v7p335#2/r5.claim: One definition distinguishes logical poetry made of false premises from conventional poetry, intentionally metered and rhymed; intention excludes accidental meter.
BURSEVI:v7p335#2/r5.anchor: قال بعضهم : الشعر إما منطقي وهو المؤلف من المقدمات

BURSEVI:v7p335#2/r6.author: İsmāʿīl Ḥaqqī Bursevī
BURSEVI:v7p335#2/r6.speaker: author
BURSEVI:v7p335#2/r6.claim: The intentionality condition excludes Quranic phrases that happen to match poetic meters, such as the cited examples from Al Imran, Saba, and Al-Saff.
BURSEVI:v7p335#2/r6.anchor: نحو قوله تعالى : {لن تنالوا البر حتى تنفقوا}

BURSEVI:v7p335#3/r1.author: İsmāʿīl Ḥaqqī Bursevī
BURSEVI:v7p335#3/r1.speaker: النبي صلى الله عليه وسلم
BURSEVI:v7p335#3/r1.claim: Several Prophetic sayings happened to scan as verse without intending meter: a line after a finger was bloodied, a couplet at Hunayn or the conquest of Mecca, and lines at the trench.
BURSEVI:v7p335#3/r1.anchor: هل أنت إلا إصبع دميت وفي سبيل الله ما لقيت وقوله يوم حنين حين نزل ودعا واستنصر

BURSEVI:v7p335#3/r2.author: İsmāʿīl Ḥaqqī Bursevī
BURSEVI:v7p335#3/r2.speaker: author
BURSEVI:v7p335#3/r2.claim: The poetry relevant to the Quran includes logical poetry, with or without meter; logical poetry often gains currency through conventional metered verse.
BURSEVI:v7p335#3/r2.anchor: والمراد بالشعر الواقع في القرآن الشعر المنطقي سواء كان مجردا عن الوزن أم لا والشعر المنطقي أكثر ما يروج بالاصطلاحي

BURSEVI:v7p335#3/r3.author: İsmāʿīl Ḥaqqī Bursevī
BURSEVI:v7p335#3/r3.speaker: الراغب
BURSEVI:v7p335#3/r3.claim: Al-Raghib says some unbelievers called the Prophet a poet because the Quran contains words with meter and rhyme.
BURSEVI:v7p335#3/r3.anchor: قال الراغب : قال بعض الكفار للنبي عليه السلام

BURSEVI:v7p335#3/r4.author: İsmāʿīl Ḥaqqī Bursevī
BURSEVI:v7p335#3/r4.speaker: بعض المحصلين
BURSEVI:v7p335#3/r4.claim: Some investigators say the accusation meant that Muhammad was a liar: the Quran plainly is not structured like poetry, and poets were associated with lying, so false arguments were called poetry.
BURSEVI:v7p335#3/r4.anchor: وقال بعض المحصلين أرادوا به أنه كاذب لأن ظاهر القرآن ليس على أساليب الشعر

BURSEVI:v7p335#3/r5.author: İsmāʿīl Ḥaqqī Bursevī
BURSEVI:v7p335#3/r5.speaker: الشريف الجرجاني
BURSEVI:v7p335#3/r5.claim: Al-Sharif al-Jurjani says people follow imaginative appeals more readily than truth when acting; poetry rests on falsehood and so is unfit for the truthful Prophet, as the saying that the best poetry is the most false suggests.
BURSEVI:v7p335#3/r5.anchor: قال الشريف الجرجاني في "حاشية المطالع" : والشعر وإن كان مفيدا للخواص والعوام

BURSEVI:v7p335#3/r6.author: İsmāʿīl Ḥaqqī Bursevī
BURSEVI:v7p335#3/r6.speaker: الشريف الجرجاني
BURSEVI:v7p335#3/r6.claim: Al-Jurjani explains that God did not teach Muhammad poetry through the Quran because revelation is elevated wisdom and law, unlike contrived meter, rhyme, and weak imaginings.
BURSEVI:v7p335#3/r6.anchor: والمعنى وما علمنا محمدا الشعر بتعليم القرآن على معنى أن القرآن ليس بشعر

BURSEVI:v7p335#3/r7.author: İsmāʿīl Ḥaqqī Bursevī
BURSEVI:v7p335#3/r7.speaker: author
BURSEVI:v7p335#3/r7.claim: The verse signals that God taught the Prophet knowledge of former and later peoples but did not teach him Satan's poetry, which Satan called his own Quran.
BURSEVI:v7p335#3/r7.anchor: وفي الآية : إشارة إلى أن النبي عليه السلام معلم من عند الله

BURSEVI:v7p336/r1.author: İsmāʿīl Ḥaqqī Bursevī
BURSEVI:v7p336/r1.speaker: الشيخ الأكبر
BURSEVI:v7p336/r1.claim: Ibn Arabi interprets poetry as a medium for ambiguity, riddling, and double meaning; God neither coded speech to Muhammad nor addressed him with hidden intended meanings he failed to grasp.
BURSEVI:v7p336/r1.anchor: قال الشيخ الأكبر قدس سره الأطهر في قوله تعالى

BURSEVI:v7p336/r2.author: İsmāʿīl Ḥaqqī Bursevī
BURSEVI:v7p336/r2.speaker: author
BURSEVI:v7p336/r2.claim: Bursevi asks how Ibn Arabi's reading relates to the disconnected letters at the suras' openings, and suggests he may not regard them as ambiguous or as knowledge reserved to God alone.
BURSEVI:v7p336/r2.anchor: وهل يشكل على هذه الحروف المقطعة في أوائل السور ولعله رضي الله عنه لا يرى أن ذلك من قبيل المتشابه

BURSEVI:v7p336/r3.author: İsmāʿīl Ḥaqqī Bursevī
BURSEVI:v7p336/r3.speaker: التأويلات النجمية
BURSEVI:v7p336/r3.claim: Al-Ta'wilat al-Najmiyya says all outward and inward human actions and states, including letters and crafts, occur through God's teaching.

BURSEVI:v7p336/r4.author: İsmāʿīl Ḥaqqī Bursevī
BURSEVI:v7p336/r4.speaker: التأويلات النجمية
BURSEVI:v7p336/r4.claim: Divine teaching occurs through intermediaries, as people teach one another, or directly, as God taught David the craft of making armor.
BURSEVI:v7p336/r4.anchor: وتعليمه الصنائع لعباده على ضربين بواسطة وبغير واسطة أما بالواسطة فبتعليم بعضهم بعضا

BURSEVI:v7p336/r5.author: İsmāʿīl Ḥaqqī Bursevī
BURSEVI:v7p336/r5.speaker: التأويلات النجمية
BURSEVI:v7p336/r5.claim: A craft a person invents through native insight without being taught by anyone is also a form of direct divine instruction.
BURSEVI:v7p336/r5.anchor: وكل حرفة وصنعة يعملها الإنسان من قريحته بغير تعليم أحد فهي من هذا القبيل

BURSEVI:v7p336/r6.author: İsmāʿīl Ḥaqqī Bursevī
BURSEVI:v7p336/r6.speaker: author
BURSEVI:v7p336/r6.claim: The Mathnawi verses say the body can learn through a master of revelation, crafts originate in revelation and are developed by reason, while some skills arise without a human teacher.
BURSEVI:v7p336/r6.anchor: قابل تعليم وفهمست اين جسد ليك صاحب وحى تعليمش دهد

BURSEVI:v7p336/r7.author: İsmāʿīl Ḥaqqī Bursevī
BURSEVI:v7p336/r7.speaker: author
BURSEVI:v7p336/r7.claim: The story of Cain says he learned to dig a grave from a crow and then buried Abel, whom he had killed and carried for days.
BURSEVI:v7p336/r7.anchor: ثم حكى قصة قابيل فإنه تعلم حفر القبر من الغراب حتى دفن أخاه هابيل بعد قتله وحمله على عاتقه أياما

BURSEVI:v7p336/r8.author: İsmāʿīl Ḥaqqī Bursevī
BURSEVI:v7p336/r8.speaker: author
BURSEVI:v7p336/r8.claim: Inbighāʾ derives from the root of seeking (ṭalab); bghaytuhu means I sought it, and it was attained.
BURSEVI:v7p336/r8.anchor: البغاء الطلب والإنبغاء انفعال منه يقال بغيته

BURSEVI:v7p336/r9.author: İsmāʿīl Ḥaqqī Bursevī
BURSEVI:v7p336/r9.speaker: الراغب
BURSEVI:v7p336/r9.claim: Al-Raghib compares ينبغي to saying fire ought to burn cloth, meaning it is made subject to burning; here poetry is neither proper nor made easy for Muhammad, even if he sought it.
BURSEVI:v7p336/r9.anchor: قال الراغب : هو مثل قوله النار ينبغي أن تحرق الثوب

BURSEVI:v7p336/r10.author: İsmāʿīl Ḥaqqī Bursevī
BURSEVI:v7p336/r10.speaker: author
BURSEVI:v7p336/r10.claim: The Prophet's tongue would break the meter through inversion or similar errors, just as his inability to write or read reinforces proof of his prophethood and removes suspicion about revelation's source.
BURSEVI:v7p336/r10.anchor: لتكون الججة أثبت وشبهة المرتابين في حقية رسالته

BURSEVI:v7p336#2/r1.author: İsmāʿīl Ḥaqqī Bursevī
BURSEVI:v7p336#2/r1.speaker: إنسان العيون
BURSEVI:v7p336#2/r1.claim: Insan al-ʿUyun says the prohibition is deliberately composing metered speech; accidentally metered words are not conventional poetry, and the Prophet usually disrupted meter when quoting a poem.
BURSEVI:v7p336#2/r1.anchor: في "إنسان العيون" والحاصل أن الحق الحقيق بالاعتماد وبه تجتمع الأقوال

BURSEVI:v7p336#2/r2.author: İsmāʿīl Ḥaqqī Bursevī
BURSEVI:v7p336#2/r2.speaker: بعض الأدباء
BURSEVI:v7p336#2/r2.claim: Some literary writers claim the Prophet could intentionally compose metered verse but did not practice it, calling this more complete than inability; Bursevi says that contradicts the Quran.
BURSEVI:v7p336#2/r2.anchor: وادعى بعض الأدباء أنه عليه السلام كان يحسن الشعر

BURSEVI:v7p336#2/r3.author: İsmāʿīl Ḥaqqī Bursevī
BURSEVI:v7p336#2/r3.speaker: البغوي
BURSEVI:v7p336#2/r3.claim: Al-Baghawi records one view that the Prophet could compose poetry but did not; the preferred view is that he could not compose it, though he could distinguish good from bad verse.
BURSEVI:v7p336#2/r3.anchor: للبغوي : من أئمتنا قيل كان عليه السلام يحسن الشعر

BURSEVI:v7p336#2/r4.author: İsmāʿīl Ḥaqqī Bursevī
BURSEVI:v7p336#2/r4.speaker: author
BURSEVI:v7p336#2/r4.claim: Bursevi suggests that the Prophet's ability to distinguish good from bad poetry may mean distinguishing metered from unmetered speech.
BURSEVI:v7p336#2/r4.anchor: ولعل المراد بين الموزون منه وغير الموزون

BURSEVI:v7p336#2/r5.author: İsmāʿīl Ḥaqqī Bursevī
BURSEVI:v7p336#2/r5.speaker: ينبوع الحياة
BURSEVI:v7p336#2/r5.claim: Yanbuʿ al-Hayah says outwardly Muslim heretics insinuated that the Prophet could compose poetry in order to undermine the Quran's denial.
BURSEVI:v7p336#2/r5.anchor: ثم رأيته في "ينبوع الحياة" قال : كان بعض الزنادقة المتظاهرين بالإسلام

BURSEVI:v7p336#2/r6.author: İsmāʿīl Ḥaqqī Bursevī
BURSEVI:v7p336#2/r6.speaker: author
BURSEVI:v7p336#2/r6.claim: Bursevi finds that defining poetry as logical falsehood but reading what is unsuitable as metrical composition makes the two clauses of the verse fail to cohere.
BURSEVI:v7p336#2/r6.anchor: وفيه إشكال كما لا يخفى على ذوي الإفهام لأنهم حين حملوا الشعر في هذا الكلام على المنطقي ثم بنوا قوله وما ينبغي له على القريض

BURSEVI:v7p336#2/r7.author: İsmāʿīl Ḥaqqī Bursevī
BURSEVI:v7p336#2/r7.speaker: author
BURSEVI:v7p336#2/r7.claim: He prefers that poetry does not befit the Prophet's prophethood and truthful nature: one taught by God speaks truth. This does not deny his natural ability to compose or distinguish verse.
BURSEVI:v7p336#2/r7.anchor: والظاهر أن المراد وما ينبغي له من حيث نبوته وصدق لهجته أن يقول الشعر لأن المعلم من عند الله لا يقول إلا حقا

BURSEVI:v7p336#2/r8.author: İsmāʿīl Ḥaqqī Bursevī
BURSEVI:v7p336#2/r8.speaker: author
BURSEVI:v7p336#2/r8.claim: Ability does not entail composing poetry; he refrained to avoid the label of poet and the suggestion of imaginative falsehood, though Arabs knew his eloquence, sweetness, and fine speech.
BURSEVI:v7p336#2/r8.anchor: لكن القدرة لا تستلزم الفعل في هذا الباب صونا عن إطلاق لفظ الشعر والشاعر الذي يوهم التخييل والكذب

IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v7p33#2/r1.author: Ibn al-Jawzī
IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v7p33#2/r1.speaker: المفسرون
IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v7p33#2/r1.claim: Exegetes say Meccan unbelievers called the Qurʾān poetry and Muhammad a poet; God answers that He did not teach him poetry and it does not come naturally to him.
IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v7p33#2/r1.anchor: قال المفسرون إن كفار مكة قالوا إن هذا القرآن شعر وإن محمدا شاعر

IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v7p33#2/r2.author: Ibn al-Jawzī
IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v7p33#2/r2.speaker: أبو بكر
IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v7p33#2/r2.claim: When Muhammad reversed a poet’s wording in a line about Islam and gray hair, Abū Bakr corrected him; the Prophet said God had not taught him poetry.
IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v7p33#2/r2.anchor: حتى إنه روي عنه صلى الله عليه وسلم أنه تمثل يوما فقال كفى بالإسلام والشيب للمرء ناهيا فقال أبو بكر يا رسول الله إنما قال الشاعر كفى الشيب والإسلام للمرء ناهيا أشهد أنك رسول الله ما علمك الله الشعر

IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v7p33#2/r3.author: Ibn al-Jawzī
IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v7p33#2/r3.speaker: أبو بكر
IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v7p33#2/r3.claim: When Muhammad recited a line to al-ʿAbbās ibn Mirdās with its two names out of order, Abū Bakr corrected it; the Prophet said either order did not matter.
IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v7p33#2/r3.anchor: ودعا يوما بعباس بن مرادس فقال أنت القائل أتجعل نهبي ونهب العبي د بين الأقرع وعيينة فقال أبو بكر بأبي أنت وأمي لم يقل كذلك فأنشده أبو بكر فقال رسول الله صلى الله عليه وسلم لا يضرك بأيهما بدأت

IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v7p33#2/r4.author: Ibn al-Jawzī
IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v7p33#2/r4.speaker: أبو بكر
IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v7p33#2/r4.claim: When the Prophet paraphrased a line about bringing news, Abū Bakr corrected the wording; Muhammad replied that he was not a poet and poetry was not fitting for him.
IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v7p33#2/r4.anchor: وتمثل يوما فقال ويأتيك من لم تزوده بالأخبار فقال أبو بكر ليس هكذا يا رسول الله فقال إني لست بشاعر ولا ينبغي لي

IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v7p33#2/r5.author: Ibn al-Jawzī
IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v7p33#2/r5.speaker: author
IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v7p33#2/r5.claim: Poetry was withheld so people would not suspect that the Qurʾān arose from Muhammad’s natural poetic skill.
IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v7p33#2/r5.anchor: وإنما منع من قول الشعر لئلا تدخل الشبهة على قوم فيما أتى به من القرآن فيقولون قوي على ذلك بما في طبعه من الفطنة للشعر

IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v7p37/r1.author: Ibn al-Jawzī
IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v7p37/r1.speaker: author
IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v7p37/r1.claim: The pronoun in “it is only” refers to the Qurʾān.
IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v7p37/r1.anchor: قوله تعالى ﴿ إن هو ﴾ يعني القرآن ﴿ إلا ذكر ﴾

IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v7p37/r3.author: Ibn al-Jawzī
IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v7p37/r3.speaker: author
IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v7p37/r3.claim: The clear Qurʾān contains duties, prophetic practices, and rulings.
IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v7p37/r3.anchor: ﴿ وقرآن مبين ﴾ فيه الفرائض والسنن والأحكام

BURSEVI:v7p337/r1.author: İsmāʿīl Ḥaqqī Bursevī
BURSEVI:v7p337/r1.speaker: author
BURSEVI:v7p337/r1.claim: The Prophet liked poetry containing wisdom, noble character, support for Islam, praise of God, or counsel to Muslims.
BURSEVI:v7p337/r1.anchor: وكان أحب الحديث إليه صلى الله عليه وسلم الشعر أي : ما كان مشتملا على حكمة أو وصف جميل

BURSEVI:v7p337/r2.author: İsmāʿīl Ḥaqqī Bursevī
BURSEVI:v7p337/r2.speaker: author
BURSEVI:v7p337/r2.claim: He disliked poetry containing falsehood, obscenity, satire, and similar faults.
BURSEVI:v7p337/r2.anchor: وأيضا كان أبغض الحديث إليه صلى الله عليه وسلم الشعر أي : ما كان فيه كذب وقبح وهجو

BURSEVI:v7p337/r3.author: İsmāʿīl Ḥaqqī Bursevī
BURSEVI:v7p337/r3.speaker: author
BURSEVI:v7p337/r3.claim: The Prophet gave Hassan a mosque pulpit to answer those who attacked him and the believers; Bursevi treats this as striving with one's tongue.
BURSEVI:v7p337/r3.anchor: وأما ما روي من أنه عليه السلام كان يضع لحسان في المسجد منبرا فيقوم عليه يهجو من كان يهجو رسول الله

BURSEVI:v7p337/r4.author: İsmāʿīl Ḥaqqī Bursevī
BURSEVI:v7p337/r4.speaker: author
BURSEVI:v7p337/r4.claim: The Qur'an is divine admonition and guidance for humans and jinn, as another verse calls it a reminder for all worlds.
BURSEVI:v7p337/r4.anchor: أي : ما القرآن {إلا ذكر} أي : عظة من الله تعالى وإرشاد للإنس والجن

BURSEVI:v7p337/r5.author: İsmāʿīl Ḥaqqī Bursevī
BURSEVI:v7p337/r5.speaker: author
BURSEVI:v7p337/r5.claim: The Qur'an is a clear heavenly book, distinguishes truth from falsehood, and brings religious success through recitation and practice.
BURSEVI:v7p337/r5.anchor: أي : كتاب سماوي بين كونه كذلك أو فارق بين الحق والباطل يقرأ في المحاريب

BURSEVI:v7p337/r6.author: İsmāʿīl Ḥaqqī Bursevī
BURSEVI:v7p337/r6.speaker: author
BURSEVI:v7p337/r6.claim: Calling the Qur'an both reminder and recitation is not redundant: the Qur'an also contains rulings and other material beyond admonition.
BURSEVI:v7p337/r6.anchor: فعطف القرآن على الذكر عطف الشيء على أحد أوصافه فإن القرآن ليس مجرد الوعظ بل هو مشتمل على المواعظ

BURSEVI:v7p337/r7.author: İsmāʿīl Ḥaqqī Bursevī
BURSEVI:v7p337/r7.speaker: كشف الأسرار
BURSEVI:v7p337/r7.claim: Kashf al-Asrar contrasts earlier prophets' visible signs with Muhammad's proof, which reaches hearts, and presents the Qur'an as his distinctive prophetic proof.
BURSEVI:v7p337/r7.anchor: قال في "كشف الأسرار" : (هريغمبرى كه آمد برهان نبوت وى ازراه ديدها در آمد وآتش ابراهيم

BURSEVI:v7p337/r8.author: İsmāʿīl Ḥaqqī Bursevī
BURSEVI:v7p337/r8.speaker: author
BURSEVI:v7p337/r8.claim: Moses challenged with his staff, Jesus with reviving the dead, and Muhammad with speech, inviting people to produce a comparable surah.
BURSEVI:v7p337/r8.anchor: إما مقصود آنست كه موسى تحدى بعصا كرد وعيسى تحدى بإحياء موتى كرد ومصطفى عليه السلام تحدى بكلام كرد

IBNKATHIR-FULL:v6p588#2/r1.author: Ibn Kathīr
IBNKATHIR-FULL:v6p588#2/r1.speaker: author
IBNKATHIR-FULL:v6p588#2/r1.claim: God did not teach Muhammad poetry, which does not suit his temperament: he neither masters nor likes it, and his nature does not incline to it.
IBNKATHIR-FULL:v6p588#2/r1.anchor: {وما علمناه الشعر وما ينبغي له} : يقول تعالى مخبرا عن نبيه محمد صلى الله عليه وسلم

IBNKATHIR-FULL:v6p588#2/r2.author: Ibn Kathīr
IBNKATHIR-FULL:v6p588#2/r2.speaker: author
IBNKATHIR-FULL:v6p588#2/r2.claim: Reports say the Prophet could not retain a regularly metered line; when he recited one, he displaced its meter or left it incomplete.
IBNKATHIR-FULL:v6p588#2/r2.anchor: كان لا يحفظ بيتا على وزن منتظم، بل إن أنشده زحفه أو لم يتمه

IBNKATHIR-FULL:v6p588#2/r3.author: Ibn Kathīr
IBNKATHIR-FULL:v6p588#2/r3.speaker: الشعبي
IBNKATHIR-FULL:v6p588#2/r3.claim: Al-Sha'bi says every child of Abd al-Muttalib recited poetry except the Messenger; Ibn Asakir included this under Utba ibn Abi Lahab, killed by a lion at al-Zarqa'.
IBNKATHIR-FULL:v6p588#2/r3.anchor: عن الشعبي أنه قال: ما ولد عبد المطلب ذكرا ولا أنثى إلا يقول الشعر، إلا رسول الله

IBNKATHIR-FULL:v6p588#2/r4.author: Ibn Kathīr
IBNKATHIR-FULL:v6p588#2/r4.speaker: الحسن البصري
IBNKATHIR-FULL:v6p588#2/r4.claim: Al-Hasan reports that the Prophet recited a line, Abu Bakr corrected its word order, and Abu Bakr or Umar recognized this as evidence he was God's Messenger.
IBNKATHIR-FULL:v6p588#2/r4.anchor: عن علي بن زيد، عن الحسن (5) -هو البصري-قال: إن رسول الله صلى الله عليه وسلم كان يتمثل بهذا البيت

IBNKATHIR-FULL:v6p588#2/r5.author: Ibn Kathīr
IBNKATHIR-FULL:v6p588#2/r5.speaker: النبي صلى الله عليه وسلم
IBNKATHIR-FULL:v6p588#2/r5.claim: Al-Bayhaqi reports the Prophet asked al-Abbas ibn Mirdas about a verse; after al-Abbas corrected the order of two names, the Prophet said the meaning was the same.
IBNKATHIR-FULL:v6p588#2/r5.anchor: وهكذا روى البيهقي في الدلائل: أن رسول الله صلى الله عليه وسلم قال:

IBNKATHIR-FULL:v6p588#2/r6.author: Ibn Kathīr
IBNKATHIR-FULL:v6p588#2/r6.speaker: السهيلي
IBNKATHIR-FULL:v6p588#2/r6.claim: Al-Suhayli explains the reordered names as honoring al-Aqra' ibn Habis above Uyayna ibn Badr, who apostatized during Abu Bakr's caliphate while al-Aqra' did not.
IBNKATHIR-FULL:v6p588#2/r6.anchor: وقد ذكر السهيلي في "الروض الأنف" لهذا التقديم والتأخير الذي وقع في كلامه، عليه السلام، في هذا البيت

IBNKATHIR-FULL:v6p588#2/r7.author: Ibn Kathīr
IBNKATHIR-FULL:v6p588#2/r7.speaker: النبي صلى الله عليه وسلم
IBNKATHIR-FULL:v6p588#2/r7.claim: Al-Umāwī reports the Prophet walking among the Badr dead and beginning a verse, which Abu Bakr then completed.
IBNKATHIR-FULL:v6p588#2/r7.anchor: وهكذا روى الأموي في مغازيه: أن رسول الله صلى الله عليه وسلم جعل يمشي بين القتلى يوم بدر

IBNKATHIR-FULL:v6p592/r1.author: Ibn Kathīr
IBNKATHIR-FULL:v6p592/r1.speaker: أبي بن كعب وبريدة بن الحصيب وعبد الله بن عباس
IBNKATHIR-FULL:v6p592/r1.claim: Abu Dawud reports the Prophet's saying that eloquence can be magic and that poetry contains wisdom.
IBNKATHIR-FULL:v6p592/r1.anchor: وقد روى أبو داود من حديث أبي بن كعب، وبريدة بن الحصيب (3) ، وعبد الله بن عباس، أن رسول الله

IBNKATHIR-FULL:v6p592/r2.author: Ibn Kathīr
IBNKATHIR-FULL:v6p592/r2.speaker: author
IBNKATHIR-FULL:v6p592/r2.claim: This is a clear reminder and Qur'an, plain to anyone who reflects and considers it carefully.
IBNKATHIR-FULL:v6p592/r2.anchor: إلا ذكر وقرآن مبين} أي: بين واضح جلي لمن تأمله وتدبره

IBNKATHIR-FULL:v6p592/r7.author: Ibn Kathīr
IBNKATHIR-FULL:v6p592/r7.speaker: author
IBNKATHIR-FULL:v6p592/r7.claim: The Qur'an is mercy for the believer and a conclusive proof against the disbeliever.
IBNKATHIR-FULL:v6p592/r7.anchor: هو رحمة للمؤمن، وحجة على الكافر

KASHSHAF-FULL:v4p28#2/r1.author: al-Zamakhsharī
KASHSHAF-FULL:v4p28#2/r1.speaker: عقبة بن أبي معيط
KASHSHAF-FULL:v4p28#2/r1.claim: The source reports that ʿUqba ibn Abi Muʿayt was the person who called the Messenger a poet.
KASHSHAF-FULL:v4p28#2/r1.anchor: كانوا يقولون لرسول الله صلى الله عليه وسلم : شاعر ، وروي أن القائل : عقبة بن أبي معيط

KASHSHAF-FULL:v4p28#2/r2.author: al-Zamakhsharī
KASHSHAF-FULL:v4p28#2/r2.speaker: author
KASHSHAF-FULL:v4p28#2/r2.claim: “We did not teach him poetry” means God did not teach poetry through the Qur’an: it is not poetry and has no relation to it.
KASHSHAF-FULL:v4p28#2/r2.anchor: أي : وما علمناه بتعليم القرآن الشعر ، على معنى : أن القرآن ليس بشعر

KASHSHAF-FULL:v4p28#2/r3.author: al-Zamakhsharī
KASHSHAF-FULL:v4p28#2/r3.speaker: author
KASHSHAF-FULL:v4p28#2/r3.claim: Poetry is metered, rhymed speech pursuing poets’ chosen meanings; the Qur’an lacks its meter, rhyme, themes, arrangement, and styles.
KASHSHAF-FULL:v4p28#2/r3.anchor: والشعر إنما هو كلام موزون مقفى ، يدل على معنى ، فأين الوزن ؟ وأين التقفية ؟

KASHSHAF-FULL:v4p28#2/r4.author: al-Zamakhsharī
KASHSHAF-FULL:v4p28#2/r4.speaker: author
KASHSHAF-FULL:v4p28#2/r4.claim: It was neither fitting nor possible for Muhammad to compose poetry: even if he tried, it would not come easily, just as he could not write, strengthening proof and dispelling doubt.
KASHSHAF-FULL:v4p28#2/r4.anchor: وما يصح له ولا يتطلب لو طلبه ، أي : جعلناه بحيث لو أراد قرض الشعر لم يتأت له

KASHSHAF-FULL:v4p28#2/r5.author: al-Zamakhsharī
KASHSHAF-FULL:v4p28#2/r5.speaker: الخليل
KASHSHAF-FULL:v4p28#2/r5.claim: Al-Khalil says poetry was dearer to the Messenger than much speech, but did not come readily to him.
KASHSHAF-FULL:v4p28#2/r5.anchor: وعن الخليل : كان الشعر أحب إلى رسول الله صلى الله عليه وسلم من كثير من الكلام ، ولكن كان لا يتأتى له

KASHSHAF-FULL:v4p28#2/r6.author: al-Zamakhsharī
KASHSHAF-FULL:v4p28#2/r6.speaker: author
KASHSHAF-FULL:v4p28#2/r6.claim: The Prophet’s “I am the prophet, no lie” and “bloodied finger” lines are natural, uncrafted speech, not deliberate poetry; accidental meter in ordinary speech is not called poetry.
KASHSHAF-FULL:v4p28#2/r6.anchor: أنا النبي لا كذب … أنا ابن عبد المطلب

KASHSHAF-FULL:v4p28#2/r7.author: al-Zamakhsharī
KASHSHAF-FULL:v4p28#2/r7.speaker: الخليل
KASHSHAF-FULL:v4p28#2/r7.claim: Al-Khalil did not count truncated rajaz as poetry, answering the objection from the Prophet’s metrical phrases.
KASHSHAF-FULL:v4p28#2/r7.anchor: على أن الخليل ما كان يعد المشطور من الرجز شعرا

KASHSHAF-FULL:v4p28#2/r8.author: al-Zamakhsharī
KASHSHAF-FULL:v4p28#2/r8.speaker: author
KASHSHAF-FULL:v4p28#2/r8.claim: The Qur’an is a reminder from God to admonish humans and jinn, and a heavenly Book recited in worship whose recitation and practice bring success, unlike poetry inspired by devils.
KASHSHAF-FULL:v4p28#2/r8.anchor: يعني : ما هو إلا ذكر من الله تعالى يوعظ به الإنس والجن ، كما قال : { إن هو إلا ذكر للعالمين }

NASAFI-FULL:v4p13#2/r1.author: al-Nasafī
NASAFI-FULL:v4p13#2/r1.speaker: مشركو قريش
NASAFI-FULL:v4p13#2/r1.claim: The deniers called the Messenger a poet, and this verse was revealed in response.
NASAFI-FULL:v4p13#2/r1.anchor: وكانوا يقولون لرسول الله صلى الله عليه وسلم شاعر فنزل

NASAFI-FULL:v4p13#2/r2.author: al-Nasafī
NASAFI-FULL:v4p13#2/r2.speaker: author
NASAFI-FULL:v4p13#2/r2.claim: God did not teach the Prophet poetry, nor did teaching him the Qur'an amount to teaching poetry: poetry is metered, rhymed speech, unlike the Qur'an on examination.
NASAFI-FULL:v4p13#2/r2.anchor: أى وما علمنا النبى عليه السلام قول الشعراء أو وما علمناه بتعليم القرآن الشعر على معنى أن القرآن ليس بشعر

NASAFI-FULL:v4p13#2/r3.author: al-Nasafī
NASAFI-FULL:v4p13#2/r3.speaker: author
NASAFI-FULL:v4p13#2/r3.claim: Poetry is neither fitting nor natural for him; even if he tried composing it, it would not come readily, just as his illiteracy strengthened the proof and defeated suspicion.
NASAFI-FULL:v4p13#2/r3.anchor: ومايصح له ولا يليق بحاله ولا يتطلب لو طلبه أى جعلناه بحيث لو أراد قرض الشعر لم يتأت له

NASAFI-FULL:v4p13#2/r4.author: al-Nasafī
NASAFI-FULL:v4p13#2/r4.speaker: author
NASAFI-FULL:v4p13#2/r4.claim: The Prophet's occasional metrically shaped phrases arose spontaneously without craft or intent; ordinary speech can accidentally scan and is not poetry without an intention to compose meter.
NASAFI-FULL:v4p13#2/r4.anchor: فما هو إلا من جنس كلامه الذي كان يرمي به على السليقة من غير صنعة فيه ولا تكلف الا انه اتفق من غير قصد

NASAFI-FULL:v4p13#2/r5.author: al-Nasafī
NASAFI-FULL:v4p13#2/r5.speaker: author
NASAFI-FULL:v4p13#2/r5.claim: In the cited lines, he pronounced laqītu with a still final tāʾ, opened the bāʾ of kadhib, and lowered the bāʾ of al-Muṭṭalib, showing the uncrafted wording.
NASAFI-FULL:v4p13#2/r5.anchor: قال لقيت بالسكون وفتح الباء في كذب وخفض الباء في المطلب

NASAFI-FULL:v4p13#2/r6.author: al-Nasafī
NASAFI-FULL:v4p13#2/r6.speaker: author
NASAFI-FULL:v4p13#2/r6.claim: The pronoun refers to what was taught: it is God's admonition for humans and jinn, and a clear heavenly book recited in prayer and worship, whose recitation and practice bring success in both worlds.
NASAFI-FULL:v4p13#2/r6.anchor: ﴿ إن هو ﴾ أي المعلم ﴿ إلا ذكر وقرآن مبين ﴾ أي ما هو إلا ذكر من الله يوعظ به الإنس والجن وما هو إلا قرآن كتاب سماوي يقرأ في المحاريب

NASAFI-FULL:v4p13#2/r7.author: al-Nasafī
NASAFI-FULL:v4p13#2/r7.speaker: author
NASAFI-FULL:v4p13#2/r7.claim: The Qur'an differs utterly from poetry, which comes from satanic promptings.
NASAFI-FULL:v4p13#2/r7.anchor: فكم بينه وبين الشعر الذي هو من همزات الشياطين

QURTUBI-FULL:36:69-70/r1.author: al-Qurṭubī
QURTUBI-FULL:36:69-70/r1.speaker: author
QURTUBI-FULL:36:69-70/r1.claim: The verse answers unbelievers who called Muhammad a poet and Qurʾan poetry; poetry was not taught to him and was unfitting.
QURTUBI-FULL:36:69-70/r1.anchor: أخبر تعالى عن حال نبيه صلى الله عليه وسلم، ورد قول من قال من الكفار إنه شاعر

QURTUBI-FULL:36:69-70/r2.author: al-Qurṭubī
QURTUBI-FULL:36:69-70/r2.speaker: النبي صلى الله عليه وسلم
QURTUBI-FULL:36:69-70/r2.claim: The Prophet did not compose or scan poetry; attempts to quote old lines broke their meter, though he preserved meaning.
QURTUBI-FULL:36:69-70/r2.anchor: وكذلك كان رسول الله صلى الله عليه وسلم لا يقول الشعر ولا يزنه، وكان إذا حاول إنشاد بيت قديم

QURTUBI-FULL:36:69-70/r3.author: al-Qurṭubī
QURTUBI-FULL:36:69-70/r3.speaker: النبي صلى الله عليه وسلم
QURTUBI-FULL:36:69-70/r3.claim: He once quoted Tarafa’s line that days reveal what one did not know.
QURTUBI-FULL:36:69-70/r3.anchor: من ذلك أنه أنشد يوما قول طرفة: ستبدي لك الأيام ما كنت جاهلا

QURTUBI-FULL:36:69-70/r4.author: al-Qurṭubī
QURTUBI-FULL:36:69-70/r4.speaker: النبي صلى الله عليه وسلم
QURTUBI-FULL:36:69-70/r4.claim: Asked who was most poetic, he quoted a line beginning ‘Do you not see me whenever I come at night?’
QURTUBI-FULL:36:69-70/r4.anchor: وأنشد يوما وقد قيل له من أشعر الناس فقال الذي يقول: ألم ترياني كلما جئت طارقا

QURTUBI-FULL:36:69-70/r5.author: al-Qurṭubī
QURTUBI-FULL:36:69-70/r5.speaker: النبي صلى الله عليه وسلم
QURTUBI-FULL:36:69-70/r5.claim: He recited a line about dividing booty between al-Aqraʿ and ʿUyayna.
QURTUBI-FULL:36:69-70/r5.anchor: وأنشد يوما: أتجعل نهبي ونهب العب

QURTUBI-FULL:36:69-70/r6.author: al-Qurṭubī
QURTUBI-FULL:36:69-70/r6.speaker: النبي صلى الله عليه وسلم
QURTUBI-FULL:36:69-70/r6.claim: On rare occasions he recited a correctly metered line by ʿAbd Allah ibn Rawaha.
QURTUBI-FULL:36:69-70/r6.anchor: روي أنه أنشد بيت عبد الله بن رواحة: يبيت يجافي جنبه عن فراشه

QURTUBI-FULL:36:69-70/r7.author: al-Qurṭubī
QURTUBI-FULL:36:69-70/r7.speaker: الحسن بن أبي الحسن
QURTUBI-FULL:36:69-70/r7.claim: Al-Hasan says the Prophet recited a line on Islam and gray hair; Abu Bakr corrected it, and Abu Bakr or ʿUmar attested his prophethood.
QURTUBI-FULL:36:69-70/r7.anchor: وقال الحسن بن أبي الحسن: أنشد النبي عليه السلام: كفى بالإسلام والشيب للمرء ناهيا

QURTUBI-FULL:36:69-70/r8.author: al-Qurṭubī
QURTUBI-FULL:36:69-70/r8.speaker: الخليل بن أحمد
QURTUBI-FULL:36:69-70/r8.claim: Al-Khalil says poetry was dear to the Prophet but did not come naturally.
QURTUBI-FULL:36:69-70/r8.anchor: وعن الخليل بن أحمد: كان الشعر أحب إلى رسول الله صلى الله عليه وسلم من كثير من الكلام

QURTUBI-FULL:36:69-70/r9.author: al-Qurṭubī
QURTUBI-FULL:36:69-70/r9.speaker: author
QURTUBI-FULL:36:69-70/r9.claim: Occasional metrical speech does not prove poetic knowledge; sayings and Qurʾanic verses such as 3:92 can fit meter.
QURTUBI-FULL:36:69-70/r9.anchor: إصابته الوزن أحيانا لا يوجب أنه يعلم الشعر

QURTUBI-FULL:36:69-70#2/r1.author: al-Qurṭubī
QURTUBI-FULL:36:69-70#2/r1.speaker: ابن العربي
QURTUBI-FULL:36:69-70#2/r1.claim: Ibn al-ʿArabi discusses Qurʾanic phrases that happen to scan, including 61:13 and 34:13, and excludes them from meter.
QURTUBI-FULL:36:69-70#2/r1.anchor: وقد ذكر ابن العربي منها آيات وتكلم عليها وأخرجها عن الوزن

QURTUBI-FULL:36:69-70#2/r2.author: al-Qurṭubī
QURTUBI-FULL:36:69-70#2/r2.speaker: الأخفش
QURTUBI-FULL:36:69-70#2/r2.claim: Al-Akhfash says ‘I am the Prophet, no lie’ is not poetry.
QURTUBI-FULL:36:69-70#2/r2.anchor: على أن أبا الحسن الأخفش قال في قوله: «أنا النبي لا كذب» ليس بشعر.

QURTUBI-FULL:36:69-70#2/r3.author: al-Qurṭubī
QURTUBI-FULL:36:69-70#2/r3.speaker: الخليل
QURTUBI-FULL:36:69-70#2/r3.claim: Al-Khalil says two-part rhymed prose is not poetry; another report from him calls the line shortened rajaz.
QURTUBI-FULL:36:69-70#2/r3.anchor: وقال الخليل في كتاب العين: إن ما جاء من السجع على جزءين لا يكون شعرا. وروي عنه أنه من منهوك الرجز.

QURTUBI-FULL:36:69-70#2/r4.author: al-Qurṭubī
QURTUBI-FULL:36:69-70#2/r4.speaker: قيل
QURTUBI-FULL:36:69-70#2/r4.claim: Another view denies shortened rajaz if the bāʾs are paused on.
QURTUBI-FULL:36:69-70#2/r4.anchor: وقد قيل: لا يكون من منهوك الرجز بالوقف على الباء

QURTUBI-FULL:36:69-70#2/r5.author: al-Qurṭubī
QURTUBI-FULL:36:69-70#2/r5.speaker: author
QURTUBI-FULL:36:69-70#2/r5.claim: It is not known how the Prophet pronounced the lines.
QURTUBI-FULL:36:69-70#2/r5.anchor: ولم يعلم كيف قاله النبي صلى الله عليه وسلم.

QURTUBI-FULL:36:69-70#2/r6.author: al-Qurṭubī
QURTUBI-FULL:36:69-70#2/r6.speaker: ابن العربي
QURTUBI-FULL:36:69-70#2/r6.claim: Ibn al-ʿArabi thinks the Prophet likely pronounced kadhib with nominative bāʾ and Muttalib genitive as annexation.
QURTUBI-FULL:36:69-70#2/r6.anchor: قال ابن العربي: والأظهر من حاله أنه قال «لا كذب» الباء مرفوعة

QURTUBI-FULL:36:69-70#3/r1.author: al-Qurṭubī
QURTUBI-FULL:36:69-70#3/r1.speaker: النحاس
QURTUBI-FULL:36:69-70#3/r1.claim: Al-Nahhas cites a view that full inflection breaks the meter.
QURTUBI-FULL:36:69-70#3/r1.anchor: وقال النحاس قال بعضهم: إنما الرواية بالإعراب، وإذا كانت بالإعراب لم يكن شعرا

QURTUBI-FULL:36:69-70#3/r2.author: al-Qurṭubī
QURTUBI-FULL:36:69-70#3/r2.speaker: author
QURTUBI-FULL:36:69-70#3/r2.claim: Qurtubi calls it denial of evident fact to say Arabs do not use that meter; al-Khalil transmitted such poetry.
QURTUBI-FULL:36:69-70#3/r2.anchor: وقال بعضهم: ليس هذا الوزن من الشعر. وهذا مكابرة العيان لأن أشعار العرب على هذا قد رواها الخليل

QURTUBI-FULL:36:69-70#3/r3.author: al-Qurṭubī
QURTUBI-FULL:36:69-70#3/r3.speaker: author
QURTUBI-FULL:36:69-70#3/r3.claim: ‘Are you anything but a bloodied finger’ scans as sariʿ only if dumiat’s tāʾ is kasra; faʿul cannot fit sariʿ.
QURTUBI-FULL:36:69-70#3/r3.anchor: وأما قوله: «هل أنت إلا إصبع دميت» فقيل إنه من بحر السريع

QURTUBI-FULL:36:69-70#3/r4.author: al-Qurṭubī
QURTUBI-FULL:36:69-70#3/r4.speaker: قيل
QURTUBI-FULL:36:69-70#3/r4.claim: Perhaps the Prophet said dumiat with still or unlengthened tāʾ, avoiding a clear poetic scan.
QURTUBI-FULL:36:69-70#3/r4.anchor: ولعل النبي صلى الله عليه وسلم قالها ساكنة التاء أو متحركة التاء من غير إشباع.

QURTUBI-FULL:36:69-70#3/r5.author: al-Qurṭubī
QURTUBI-FULL:36:69-70#3/r5.speaker: author
QURTUBI-FULL:36:69-70#3/r5.claim: Even conceding poetry, rare quotation or a couple of rajaz rhymes does not make him poet or learned in poetry.
QURTUBI-FULL:36:69-70#3/r5.anchor: ولا يلزم منه أن يكون النبي صلى الله عليه وسلم عالما بالشعر ولا شاعر أن التمثل

QURTUBI-FULL:36:69-70#3/r6.author: al-Qurṭubī
QURTUBI-FULL:36:69-70#3/r6.speaker: الزجاج والنحاس
QURTUBI-FULL:36:69-70#3/r6.claim: Al-Zajjaj says ‘not taught poetry’ means ‘not made a poet,’ not that recitation is impossible; al-Nahhas calls this excellent.
QURTUBI-FULL:36:69-70#3/r6.anchor: قال أبو إسحاق الزجاج: معنى «وما علمناه الشعر» وما علمناه أن يشعر أي ما جعلناه شاعرا

QURTUBI-FULL:36:69-70#3/r7.author: al-Qurṭubī
QURTUBI-FULL:36:69-70#3/r7.speaker: قيل
QURTUBI-FULL:36:69-70#3/r7.claim: A literal view says God reports not teaching poetry, not that the Prophet never recited it.
QURTUBI-FULL:36:69-70#3/r7.anchor: وقد قيل: إنما خبر الله عز وجل أنه ما علمه الله الشعر

QURTUBI-FULL:36:69-70#3/r8.author: al-Qurṭubī
QURTUBI-FULL:36:69-70#3/r8.speaker: قيل
QURTUBI-FULL:36:69-70#3/r8.claim: A view claimed as linguistic consensus says metrical speech is not poetry without intent; God denied knowledge of poetic forms and craft.
QURTUBI-FULL:36:69-70#3/r8.anchor: وقيل فيه قول بين زعم صاحبه أنه إجماع من أهل اللغة، وذلك أنهم قالوا: كل من قال قولا موزونا

QURTUBI-FULL:36:69-70#3/r9.author: al-Qurṭubī
QURTUBI-FULL:36:69-70#3/r9.speaker: قريش
QURTUBI-FULL:36:69-70#3/r9.claim: Perceptive Quraysh members said the poet accusation would fail because the Qurʾan resembles no known poetic genre.
QURTUBI-FULL:36:69-70#3/r9.anchor: ألا ترى أن قريشا تراوضت فيما يقولون للعرب فيه إذا قدموا عليهم الموسم

QURTUBI-FULL:36:69-70#3/r10.author: al-Qurṭubī
QURTUBI-FULL:36:69-70#3/r10.speaker: أنيس
QURTUBI-FULL:36:69-70#3/r10.claim: Anis tested the Prophet’s words against poetic meters and they did not fit; Muslim transmits this and Anis was a leading poet.
QURTUBI-FULL:36:69-70#3/r10.anchor: وقال أنيس أخو أبي ذر: لقد وضعت قوله على أقراء الشعر فلم يلتئم أنه شعر.

QURTUBI-FULL:36:69-70#3/r11.author: al-Qurṭubī
QURTUBI-FULL:36:69-70#3/r11.speaker: عتبة بن ربيعة
QURTUBI-FULL:36:69-70#3/r11.claim: ʿUtba said the Qurʾan was neither poetry, soothsaying, nor magic; others agreed.
QURTUBI-FULL:36:69-70#3/r11.anchor: وكذلك عتبة بن أبي ربيعة لما كلمه: والله ما هو بشعر ولا كهانة ولا سحر

QURTUBI-FULL:36:69-70#3/r12.author: al-Qurṭubī
QURTUBI-FULL:36:69-70#3/r12.speaker: author
QURTUBI-FULL:36:69-70#3/r12.claim: Metrical speech is not poetry without intent; accidental examples are not verses.
QURTUBI-FULL:36:69-70#3/r12.anchor: ثم إن ما يجري على اللسان من موزون الكلام لا يعد شعرا

QURTUBI-FULL:36:69-70#4/r1.author: al-Qurṭubī
QURTUBI-FULL:36:69-70#4/r1.speaker: author
QURTUBI-FULL:36:69-70#4/r1.claim: An anecdote describes a rational layman, ill, asking for a physician and to be told that he had been cauterized.
QURTUBI-FULL:36:69-70#4/r1.anchor: وقد كان رجل ينادي في مرضه وهو من عرض العامة العقلاء

QURTUBI-FULL:36:69-70#4/r2.author: al-Qurṭubī
QURTUBI-FULL:36:69-70#4/r2.speaker: مالك
QURTUBI-FULL:36:69-70#4/r2.claim: Ibn al-Qasim reports Malik advised against frequent poetry recitation, citing this verse among poetry’s faults.
QURTUBI-FULL:36:69-70#4/r2.anchor: روى ابن القاسم عن مالك أنه سئل عن إنشاد الشعر فقال: لا تكثرن منه

QURTUBI-FULL:36:69-70#4/r3.author: al-Qurṭubī
QURTUBI-FULL:36:69-70#4/r3.speaker: عمر بن الخطاب
QURTUBI-FULL:36:69-70#4/r3.claim: Umar wrote to Abu Musa to gather local poets and ask about poetry; Labid said he had written none since hearing the opening of al-Baqara.
QURTUBI-FULL:36:69-70#4/r3.anchor: بلغني أن عمر بن الخطاب رضي الله عنه كتب إلى أبي موسى الأشعري

QURTUBI-FULL:36:69-70#4/r4.author: al-Qurṭubī
QURTUBI-FULL:36:69-70#4/r4.speaker: ابن العربي
QURTUBI-FULL:36:69-70#4/r4.claim: Ibn al-Arabi says denying poetry to the Prophet is no criticism of poetry, just as his not writing is no criticism of writing.
QURTUBI-FULL:36:69-70#4/r4.anchor: قال ابن العربي: هذه الآية ليست من عيب الشعر كما لم يكن قوله

QURTUBI-FULL:36:69-70#4/r5.author: al-Qurṭubī
QURTUBI-FULL:36:69-70#4/r5.speaker: المأمون
QURTUBI-FULL:36:69-70#4/r5.claim: Al-Mamun told Abu Ali al-Minqari that the Prophet’s illiteracy and inability to compose verse were virtues for him but deficiencies in the other man.
QURTUBI-FULL:36:69-70#4/r5.anchor: روى أن المأمون قال لأبي علي المنقري: بلغني أنك أمي، وأنك لا تقيم الشعر

QURTUBI-FULL:36:69-70#4/r6.author: al-Qurṭubī
QURTUBI-FULL:36:69-70#4/r6.speaker: author
QURTUBI-FULL:36:69-70#4/r6.claim: God withheld poetry and writing from the Prophet to remove suspicion that natural poetic ability produced the Qur’an, not because poetry or writing is defective.
QURTUBI-FULL:36:69-70#4/r6.anchor: وإنما منع النبي صلى الله عليه وسلم ذلك لنفي الظنة عنه، لا لعيب في الشعر والكتابة

QURTUBI-FULL:36:69-70#4/r7.author: al-Qurṭubī
QURTUBI-FULL:36:69-70#4/r7.speaker: author
QURTUBI-FULL:36:69-70#4/r7.claim: Accidental agreement with poetic meter does not make Qur’anic or Prophetic speech poetry; otherwise any ordinary person speaking metrically would be a poet.
QURTUBI-FULL:36:69-70#4/r7.anchor: لأن ما وافق وزنه وزن الشعر، ولم يقصد به إلى الشعر ليس بشعر

QURTUBI-FULL:36:69-70#4/r8.author: al-Qurṭubī
QURTUBI-FULL:36:69-70#4/r8.speaker: الزجاج
QURTUBI-FULL:36:69-70#4/r8.claim: Al-Zajjaj explains that poetry was not made easy for the Prophet to say, rather than that he could not compose it.
QURTUBI-FULL:36:69-70#4/r8.anchor: وقال الزجاج: معنى «وما ينبغي له» أي ما يتسهل له قول الشعر لا الإنشاء

QURTUBI-FULL:36:69-70#4/r9.author: al-Qurṭubī
QURTUBI-FULL:36:69-70#4/r9.speaker: author
QURTUBI-FULL:36:69-70#4/r9.claim: The recitation delivered to the audience is only a reminder and a clear Qur’an.

RAZI-FULL:v26p91#3/r1.author: Fakhr al-Dīn al-Rāzī
RAZI-FULL:v26p91#3/r1.speaker: author
RAZI-FULL:v26p91#3/r1.claim: After treating two of the three principles, oneness and resurrection, the passage turns to the third, prophethood: oneness appears in the ban on serving Satan and the command to worship God, and resurrection in the scenes of Hell and sealed mouths.

RAZI-FULL:v26p91#3/r2.author: Fakhr al-Dīn al-Rāzī
RAZI-FULL:v26p91#3/r2.speaker: author
RAZI-FULL:v26p91#3/r2.claim: Saying God did not teach Muhammad poetry indicates that God teaches him what He wills and does not teach what He does not will.
RAZI-FULL:v26p91#3/r2.anchor: إشارة إلى أنه معلم من عند الله فعلمه ما أراد ولم يعلمه ما لم يرد

RAZI-FULL:v26p91#3/r3.author: Fakhr al-Dīn al-Rāzī
RAZI-FULL:v26p91#3/r3.speaker: author
RAZI-FULL:v26p91#3/r3.claim: The verse singles out poetry because Muhammad's opponents called him a diviner when his reports of the unseen came true, a magician when he performed miracles, and a poet when he recited the Qur'an; only the Qur'an was his challenge to them, so poetry is denied specifically.

RAZI-FULL:v26p92/r1.author: Fakhr al-Dīn al-Rāzī
RAZI-FULL:v26p92/r1.speaker: قوم
RAZI-FULL:v26p92/r1.claim: One reported interpretation is that poetry did not come naturally to Muhammad.
RAZI-FULL:v26p92/r1.anchor: قال قوم ما كان يتأتي له

RAZI-FULL:v26p92/r2.author: Fakhr al-Dīn al-Rāzī
RAZI-FULL:v26p92/r2.speaker: آخرون
RAZI-FULL:v26p92/r2.claim: Another interpretation is that poetry did not come easily to him, so any verse he attempted would have defective meter.
RAZI-FULL:v26p92/r2.anchor: وآخرون ما يتسهل له حتى أنه إن تمثل بيت شعر سمع منه مزاحفا

RAZI-FULL:v26p92/r3.author: Fakhr al-Dīn al-Rāzī
RAZI-FULL:v26p92/r3.speaker: النبي صلى الله عليه وسلم
RAZI-FULL:v26p92/r3.claim: A report says that when Muhammad recited the line “And news will come to you from one you did not provide for,” its meter was defective, offered as evidence that poetry was not easy for him.
RAZI-FULL:v26p92/r3.anchor: كان يقول صلى الله عليه وسلم

RAZI-FULL:v26p92/r4.author: Fakhr al-Dīn al-Rāzī
RAZI-FULL:v26p92/r4.speaker: author
RAZI-FULL:v26p92/r4.claim: Al-Razi prefers the plain sense that poetry does not befit Muhammad: a lawgiver's wording follows the intended meaning, whereas a poet's meaning follows diction chosen first to satisfy meter or rhyme.
RAZI-FULL:v26p92/r4.anchor: على مفهومه الظاهر وهو أن الشعر ما كان يليق به

RAZI-FULL:v26p92/r5.author: Fakhr al-Dīn al-Rāzī
RAZI-FULL:v26p92/r5.speaker: author
RAZI-FULL:v26p92/r5.claim: Poetry is metered speech whose meter is intended primarily; if a speaker aims first at meaning and the result happens to be metered and rhymed, it is not poetry.
RAZI-FULL:v26p92/r5.anchor: الشعر هو الكلام الموزون الذي قصد إلى وزنه قصدا أوليا

RAZI-FULL:v26p92/r6.author: Fakhr al-Dīn al-Rāzī
RAZI-FULL:v26p92/r6.speaker: author
RAZI-FULL:v26p92/r6.claim: Qur'an 3:92 is not poetry although it can be scanned in a poetic meter: the wise person seeks the meaning first, while a poet selects words first to fit the meter and makes meaning follow them.
RAZI-FULL:v26p92/r6.anchor: لن تنالوا البر حتى تنفقوا مما تحبون

RAZI-FULL:v26p92/r7.author: Fakhr al-Dīn al-Rāzī
RAZI-FULL:v26p92/r7.speaker: author
RAZI-FULL:v26p92/r7.claim: Muhammad's occasional utterance of a metrical line, including “I am the Prophet, no lie; I am the son of Abd al-Muttalib,” does not make him a poet because he did not intend meter and rhyme first; even much accidentally metrical speech would not do so.
RAZI-FULL:v26p92/r7.anchor: أنا النبي لا كذب … أنا ابن عبد المطلب

RAZI-FULL:v26p92/r8.author: Fakhr al-Dīn al-Rāzī
RAZI-FULL:v26p92/r8.speaker: author
RAZI-FULL:v26p92/r8.claim: Ordinary market speech can scan as a poetic meter without being poetry, since its speakers did not first intend the wording for meter or rhyme.
RAZI-FULL:v26p92/r8.anchor: إذا تتبعت كلام الناس في الأسواق تجد فيه ما يكون موزونا واقعا في بحر من بحور الشعر ولا يسمى المتكلم به شاعرا

RAZI-FULL:v26p92/r9.author: Fakhr al-Dīn al-Rāzī
RAZI-FULL:v26p92/r9.speaker: author
RAZI-FULL:v26p92/r9.claim: The contrast is between the Qur'an as reminder and admonition aimed at meaning and poetry as speech embellished by rhyme and meter.
RAZI-FULL:v26p92/r9.anchor: هو ذكر وموعظة للقصد إلى المعنى

RAZI-FULL:v26p92/r10.author: Fakhr al-Dīn al-Rāzī
RAZI-FULL:v26p92/r10.speaker: النبي صلى الله عليه وسلم
RAZI-FULL:v26p92/r10.claim: The Prophet said that some poetry contains wisdom: a poet may intend wording and happen upon a wise meaning, while a sage may intend meaning and happen upon meter; neither thereby becomes the other kind of speaker.
RAZI-FULL:v26p92/r10.anchor: النبي صلى الله عليه وسلم قال : ( إن من الشعر لحكمة

RAZI-FULL:v26p92/r11.author: Fakhr al-Dīn al-Rāzī
RAZI-FULL:v26p92/r11.speaker: author
RAZI-FULL:v26p92/r11.claim: Meaning is the heart and spirit of wording, while wording is its form; a sage's metrical speech remains wisdom, and a poet's admonition may convey wisdom, so meter does not negate the message's substance.
RAZI-FULL:v26p92/r11.anchor: قلب اللفظ وروحه فإذا وجد القلب لا نظر إلى القالب

STUDYQURAN:36:69/r1.author: Seyyed Hossein Nasr (ed.-in-chief), Caner K. Dagli, Maria Massi Dakake, Joseph E. B. Lumbard, Mohammed Rustom
STUDYQURAN:36:69/r1.speaker: author
STUDYQURAN:36:69/r1.claim: The verse returns to the sūrah’s opening discussion of revelation and recalls the accusations that Muhammad was a poet.
STUDYQURAN:36:69/r1.anchor: the nature of revelation from the beginning of the sūrah

STUDYQURAN:36:69/r2.author: Seyyed Hossein Nasr (ed.-in-chief), Caner K. Dagli, Maria Massi Dakake, Joseph E. B. Lumbard, Mohammed Rustom
STUDYQURAN:36:69/r2.speaker: IK, Q
STUDYQURAN:36:69/r2.claim: IK and Q report that the Prophet had no facility with poetry, including its rhyme or meter.
STUDYQURAN:36:69/r2.anchor: the Prophet did not have any facility with poetry, either its rhyme or meter (IK, Q)

STUDYQURAN:36:69/r3.author: Seyyed Hossein Nasr (ed.-in-chief), Caner K. Dagli, Maria Massi Dakake, Joseph E. B. Lumbard, Mohammed Rustom
STUDYQURAN:36:69/r3.speaker: author
STUDYQURAN:36:69/r3.claim: The charge that Muhammad authored the Quran is answered at 29:48: he had not recited a book or written with his right hand.
STUDYQURAN:36:69/r3.anchor: Regarding the accusations that the Prophet had himself authored the Quran, 29:48 replies

STUDYQURAN:36:69/r4.author: Seyyed Hossein Nasr (ed.-in-chief), Caner K. Dagli, Maria Massi Dakake, Joseph E. B. Lumbard, Mohammed Rustom
STUDYQURAN:36:69/r4.speaker: author
STUDYQURAN:36:69/r4.claim: The Quran is repeatedly described as a reminder in 6:69, 6:90, 12:104, 38:87, 68:52, 74:31, and 81:27.
STUDYQURAN:36:69/r4.anchor: That the Quran is but a reminder is repeated in several verses

STUDYQURAN:36:69/r5.author: Seyyed Hossein Nasr (ed.-in-chief), Caner K. Dagli, Maria Massi Dakake, Joseph E. B. Lumbard, Mohammed Rustom
STUDYQURAN:36:69/r5.speaker: author
STUDYQURAN:36:69/r5.claim: Reminding is revelation’s function: the Torah is a Reminder, and Jews and Christians are called the people of the Reminder.
STUDYQURAN:36:69/r5.anchor: To remind is the function of all revelation; hence the Torah is called a Reminder (40:54)

STUDYQURAN:36:69/r6.author: Seyyed Hossein Nasr (ed.-in-chief), Caner K. Dagli, Maria Massi Dakake, Joseph E. B. Lumbard, Mohammed Rustom
STUDYQURAN:36:69/r6.speaker: author
STUDYQURAN:36:69/r6.claim: The Quran continues earlier Reminders and clarifies what people may have forgotten; 16:44 says it was sent down to clarify revelation for mankind.
STUDYQURAN:36:69/r6.anchor: the Quran is presented as a continuation of the previous Reminders that clarifies what humans may have forgotten from them

TAB-FULL:v19p480/r1.author: al-Ṭabarī
TAB-FULL:v19p480/r1.speaker: author
TAB-FULL:v19p480/r1.claim: God did not teach Muhammad poetry, and it is unfitting for him to be a poet.
TAB-FULL:v19p480/r1.anchor: عن قتادة، قوله: {وما علمناه الشعر وما ينبغي له} [يس: 69] قال: " قيل لعائشة: هل كان رسول الله صلى الله عليه وسلم يتمثل بشيء من الشعر

TAB-FULL:v19p480/r2.author: al-Ṭabarī
TAB-FULL:v19p480/r2.speaker: عائشة
TAB-FULL:v19p480/r2.claim: Aisha says poetry was the Prophet's most disliked speech; he sometimes recited a Banu Qays verse backward, and after Abu Bakr corrected it he said he was no poet.
TAB-FULL:v19p480/r2.anchor: عن قتادة، قوله: {وما علمناه الشعر وما ينبغي له} [يس: 69] قال: " قيل لعائشة: هل كان رسول الله صلى الله عليه وسلم يتمثل بشيء من الشعر

TAB-FULL:v19p480#2/r1.author: al-Ṭabarī
TAB-FULL:v19p480#2/r1.speaker: author
TAB-FULL:v19p480#2/r1.claim: Al-Tabari identifies Muhammad as the reminder sent to people; the associated message is the Quran, which Qatada also identifies as this Quran.

TAB-FULL:v19p480#2/r2.author: al-Ṭabarī
TAB-FULL:v19p480#2/r2.speaker: author
TAB-FULL:v19p480#2/r2.claim: The Quran Muhammad brought makes clear to thoughtful people that it is revelation from God, not poetry or soothsayer speech.

TAB-FULL:v19p480#2/r3.author: al-Ṭabarī
TAB-FULL:v19p480#2/r3.speaker: قتادة
TAB-FULL:v19p480#2/r3.claim: Qatada identifies the phrase as this Quran.

SULAMI:v2p174#3/r1.author: al-Sulamī
SULAMI:v2p174#3/r1.speaker: سهل
SULAMI:v2p174#3/r1.claim: The Qur’an is reminder and reflection for those able to understand it, take heed from its admonitions, and obey its commands.
SULAMI:v2p174#3/r1.anchor: قال سهل : هو التذكر والتفكر لمن قاربه فهمه واتعظ بمواعظه

TUSTARI:36:69/r1.author: Sahl al-Tustarī
TUSTARI:36:69/r1.speaker: author
TUSTARI:36:69/r1.claim: The verse's 'remembrance' means remembrance and reflection.

TABATABAI:36:69-71/r1.author: Muḥammad Ḥusayn al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī
TABATABAI:36:69-71/r1.speaker: author
TABATABAI:36:69-71/r1.claim: Not teaching the Prophet poetry means he was not able to compose it; it does not mean he could compose it but abstained because God forbade him.
TABATABAI:36:69-71/r1.anchor: نفي أن يكون علمه الشعر ولازمه أن يكون بحيث لا يحسن قول الشعر

TABATABAI:36:69-71/r2.author: Muḥammad Ḥusayn al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī
TABATABAI:36:69-71/r2.speaker: author
TABATABAI:36:69-71/r2.claim: The phrase wards off an inference of deficiency or incapacity: God raised and purified the Prophet beyond poetry's invented embellishments and musical meters, fitting his mission and the inimitable Quran.
TABATABAI:36:69-71/r2.anchor: فالجملة في مقام دفع الدخل والمحصل أن عدم تعليمنا إياه الشعر ليس يوجب نقصا فيه ولا أنه تعجيز له

TABATABAI:36:69-71/r3.author: Muḥammad Ḥusayn al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī
TABATABAI:36:69-71/r3.speaker: author
TABATABAI:36:69-71/r3.claim: The restrictive construction is قصر القلب: the Quran is not poetry; it is a reminder and a clear Quran.
TABATABAI:36:69-71/r3.anchor: فالحصر المستفاد من قوله { إن هو إلا ذكر } الخ من قصر القلب

TABRISI:36:69-70/r1.author: al-Ṭabrisī
TABRISI:36:69-70/r1.speaker: author
TABRISI:36:69-70/r1.claim: What was revealed is a reminder and clear Qur’an from the Lord of the worlds, not poetry, rajaz, or a sermon.
TABRISI:36:69-70/r1.anchor: ليس بشعر ولا رجز ولا خطبة والمراد بالذكر أنه يتضمن ذكر الحلال والحرام

TABRISI:36:69-70/r2.author: al-Ṭabrisī
TABRISI:36:69-70/r2.speaker: author
TABRISI:36:69-70/r2.claim: It is a reminder because it contains rulings, proofs, and accounts of past nations; it is Qur’an because its parts are gathered together, so the two terms have distinct benefits.
TABRISI:36:69-70/r2.anchor: وبالقرآن أنه مجموع بعضه إلى بعض فجمع سبحانه بينهما لاختلاف فائدتهما

WAHIDI-BASIT:v18p517#2/r1.author: al-Wāḥidī
WAHIDI-BASIT:v18p517#2/r1.speaker: الكلبي ومقاتل
WAHIDI-BASIT:v18p517#2/r1.claim: Al-Kalbī and Muqātil report that the verse was revealed about Meccan polytheists who called the Qurʾān poetry and Muḥammad a poet, sorcerer, and liar; God refuted them.
WAHIDI-BASIT:v18p517#2/r1.anchor: قال الكلبي (¬2) ومقاتل (¬3): نزلت في مشركي مكة، حين قالوا: إن القرآن شعر

WAHIDI-BASIT:v18p517#2/r2.author: al-Wāḥidī
WAHIDI-BASIT:v18p517#2/r2.speaker: ابن عباس
WAHIDI-BASIT:v18p517#2/r2.claim: Ibn ʿAbbās says poetry was not fitting for the Prophet: he could not recite a line or make its meter come out correctly.
WAHIDI-BASIT:v18p517#2/r2.anchor: قال ابن عباس: يريد ما (¬4) ينبغي له الشعر، ما كان يروي بيت شعر ولا يقومه مستقيما

WAHIDI-BASIT:v18p517#2/r3.author: al-Wāḥidī
WAHIDI-BASIT:v18p517#2/r3.speaker: أبو إسحاق
WAHIDI-BASIT:v18p517#2/r3.claim: Abū Isḥāq glosses it as something that does not come easily to him.
WAHIDI-BASIT:v18p517#2/r3.anchor: قال أبو إسحاق: وما يتسهل ذلك

WAHIDI-BASIT:v18p517#2/r4.author: al-Wāḥidī
WAHIDI-BASIT:v18p517#2/r4.speaker: author
WAHIDI-BASIT:v18p517#2/r4.claim: Yanbaghī derives from seeking: when something sought becomes easy and comes about, it is said to be yanbaghī, as in “I broke it and it broke.”
WAHIDI-BASIT:v18p517#2/r4.anchor: وأصل (ينبغي) من قولهم: بغيت الشيء أبغيه، أي: طلبته

WAHIDI-BASIT:v18p517#2/r5.author: al-Wāḥidī
WAHIDI-BASIT:v18p517#2/r5.speaker: العباس بن مرداس
WAHIDI-BASIT:v18p517#2/r5.claim: A report says the Prophet recited al-ʿAbbās b. Mirdās’s line about dividing the spoils of Banū ʿUbayd and did not put it into correct meter.
WAHIDI-BASIT:v18p517#2/r5.anchor: فقد روي أنه كان يتمثل بقول العباس بن مرداس فيقول: أتجعل نهبي ونهب العبيد

WAHIDI-BASIT:v18p517#2/r6.author: al-Wāḥidī
WAHIDI-BASIT:v18p517#2/r6.speaker: عبد بني الحسحاس
WAHIDI-BASIT:v18p517#2/r6.claim: A report says the Prophet also quoted a line by ʿAbd Banī al-Ḥasḥās with its meter broken.
WAHIDI-BASIT:v18p517#2/r6.anchor: وكان يتمثل بقول عبد بني الحسحاس (¬2) يقول: كلي (¬3) الإسلام والشيب للمرء ناهيا

WAHIDI-BASIT:v18p517#2/r7.author: al-Wāḥidī
WAHIDI-BASIT:v18p517#2/r7.speaker: طرفة
WAHIDI-BASIT:v18p517#2/r7.claim: A report says the Prophet quoted Ṭarafa’s line about news coming to one who was not provisioned, and others corrected its meter for him.
WAHIDI-BASIT:v18p517#2/r7.anchor: وكان يتكلم ببيت طرفة فيقول: ويأتيك من لم تزود بالأخبار (¬5) # فيعاد عليه مستويا

WAHIDI-BASIT:v18p517#2/r8.author: al-Wāḥidī
WAHIDI-BASIT:v18p517#2/r8.speaker: المفسرون
WAHIDI-BASIT:v18p517#2/r8.claim: The exegetes say the Prophet could not readily compose a metered line himself, based on the statement that poetry was not fitting for him.
WAHIDI-BASIT:v18p517#2/r8.anchor: والمفسرون ذهبوا إلى أنه ما كان يتسهل له أن يأتي ببيت موزون

WAHIDI-BASIT:v18p517#2/r9.author: al-Wāḥidī
WAHIDI-BASIT:v18p517#2/r9.speaker: author
WAHIDI-BASIT:v18p517#2/r9.claim: Reports also attribute to the Prophet the rajaz phrases “Are you only a finger that has been bloodied?” and “Here I am; truly the life is the life of the Hereafter.”
WAHIDI-BASIT:v18p517#2/r9.anchor: وما روي عنه من الأراجز كقوله: "هل أنت إلا أصبع دميت" (¬2)

WAHIDI-BASIT:v18p517#2/r10.author: al-Wāḥidī
WAHIDI-BASIT:v18p517#2/r10.speaker: author
WAHIDI-BASIT:v18p517#2/r10.claim: Rajaz is a kind of speech, not poetry.
WAHIDI-BASIT:v18p517#2/r10.anchor: فالرجز جنس من الكلام ليس بشعر

WAHIDI-BASIT:v18p517#2/r11.author: al-Wāḥidī
WAHIDI-BASIT:v18p517#2/r11.speaker: أبو إسحاق
WAHIDI-BASIT:v18p517#2/r11.claim: Abū Isḥāq says the verse does not require that the Prophet never quoted poetry; it means he was no poet and that the Qurʾān differs from created speech and Arab meters.
WAHIDI-BASIT:v18p517#2/r11.anchor: قال أبو إسحاق: (ليس يوجب هذا أن يكون النبي -صلى الله عليه وسلم- لم يتمثل ببيت شعر قط

WAHIDI-BASIT:v18p517#2/r12.author: al-Wāḥidī
WAHIDI-BASIT:v18p517#2/r12.speaker: أبو إسحاق
WAHIDI-BASIT:v18p517#2/r12.claim: On Abū Isḥāq’s explanation, composing poetry on his own was not easy for the Prophet.
WAHIDI-BASIT:v18p517#2/r12.anchor: وعلى ما ذكر قوله: {وما ينبغي له} معناه: وما يسهل له إنشاء الشعر من قبل نفسه

WAHIDI-BASIT:v18p520/r1.author: al-Wāḥidī
WAHIDI-BASIT:v18p520/r1.speaker: مقاتل
WAHIDI-BASIT:v18p520/r1.claim: Muqātil says “it” refers to the Qurʾān.

WAHIDI-BASIT:v18p520/r2.author: al-Wāḥidī
WAHIDI-BASIT:v18p520/r2.speaker: ابن عباس
WAHIDI-BASIT:v18p520/r2.claim: Ibn ʿAbbās glosses dhikr as an admonition.

WAHIDI-BASIT:v18p520/r3.author: al-Wāḥidī
WAHIDI-BASIT:v18p520/r3.speaker: ابن عباس
WAHIDI-BASIT:v18p520/r3.claim: Ibn ʿAbbās says the clear Qurʾān contains obligations, legal penalties, and rulings.
WAHIDI-BASIT:v18p520/r3.anchor: قال ابن عباس: موعظة. {وقرآن مبين} قال: يريد فيه الفرائض والحدود والأحكام

YAHYA-SALLAM:v2p818/r1.author: Yaḥyā b. Sallām
YAHYA-SALLAM:v2p818/r1.speaker: author
YAHYA-SALLAM:v2p818/r1.claim: It is not fitting for the Prophet to be a poet or to recite poetry.
YAHYA-SALLAM:v2p818/r1.anchor: أن يكون شاعرا ولا يروي الشعر

YAHYA-SALLAM:v2p818/r2.author: Yaḥyā b. Sallām
YAHYA-SALLAM:v2p818/r2.speaker: عائشة
YAHYA-SALLAM:v2p818/r2.claim: Aisha says the Prophet never spoke a verse of poetry, though once he tried to recite a poet’s line and could not complete it.
YAHYA-SALLAM:v2p818/r2.anchor: أن عائشة قالت: لم يتكلم رسول الله صلى الله عليه وسلم ببيت شعر قط غير أنه أراد مرة

YAHYA-SALLAM:v2p818/r3.author: Yaḥyā b. Sallām
YAHYA-SALLAM:v2p818/r3.speaker: author
YAHYA-SALLAM:v2p818/r3.claim: Yahya thinks the poet whose line the Prophet attempted was al-A‘sha.

YAHYA-SALLAM:v2p818/r4.author: Yaḥyā b. Sallām
YAHYA-SALLAM:v2p818/r4.speaker: بعضهم
YAHYA-SALLAM:v2p818/r4.claim: Some identify the poet whose line was attempted as Tarafa, rather than al-A‘sha.

YAHYA-SALLAM:v2p818/r5.author: Yaḥyā b. Sallām
YAHYA-SALLAM:v2p818/r5.speaker: أبان العطار
YAHYA-SALLAM:v2p818/r5.claim: Aban al-Attar or another narrator reports the Prophet invoking God against Tarafa for the line, correcting its wording when told the final phrase, then saying the two wordings were equivalent.
YAHYA-SALLAM:v2p818/r5.anchor: أبان العطار أو غيره أن رسول الله صلى الله عليه وسلم قال: " قاتل الله طرفة حيث يقول: ستبدي لك الأيام ما كنت جاهلا

YAHYA-SALLAM:v2p818/r6.author: Yaḥyā b. Sallām
YAHYA-SALLAM:v2p818/r6.speaker: author
YAHYA-SALLAM:v2p818/r6.claim: Inna huwa here means ma huwa, introducing the statement that it is only a reminder and clear Quran.

YAHYA-SALLAM:v2p818/r7.author: Yaḥyā b. Sallām
YAHYA-SALLAM:v2p818/r7.speaker: author
YAHYA-SALLAM:v2p818/r7.claim: The reminder is reflection for the worlds, for those among jinn and humans who believe.
YAHYA-SALLAM:v2p818/r7.anchor: يعني: ما هو إلا تفكر للعالمين لمن آمن من الجن والإنس.

YAHYA-SALLAM:v2p818/r8.author: Yaḥyā b. Sallām
YAHYA-SALLAM:v2p818/r8.speaker: الحسن
YAHYA-SALLAM:v2p818/r8.claim: Al-Hasan says it is a reminder by which people remember Paradise.
YAHYA-SALLAM:v2p818/r8.anchor: وقال الحسن: {إن هو إلا ذكر} [يس: 69] يذكرون به الجنة.

YAHYA-SALLAM:v2p818/r9.author: Yaḥyā b. Sallām
YAHYA-SALLAM:v2p818/r9.speaker: بعضهم
YAHYA-SALLAM:v2p818/r9.claim: Some say it is a reminder concerning God, with a Quran made clear.
YAHYA-SALLAM:v2p818/r9.anchor: وقال بعضهم: {إن هو إلا ذكر} [يس: 69] تذكر في ذات الله {وقرءان مبين} [يس: 69] بين.

KURANYOLU-TEFSIR:36:69/r1.author: Hayreddin Karaman, Mustafa Çağrıcı, İbrahim Kâfi Dönmez, Sadrettin Gümüş
KURANYOLU-TEFSIR:36:69/r1.speaker: author
KURANYOLU-TEFSIR:36:69/r1.claim: The initial statement may sound like a denigration of poetry, but in that period “poet” also suggested a person connected to the unseen, not merely a skilled artist.
KURANYOLU-TEFSIR:36:69/r1.anchor: o dönemde şair kelimesi sadece şiir sanatında becerisi olanlar için değil, aynı zamanda görünmeyen âlemle irtibatları bulunan kişiler hakkında da kullanılıyordu

KURANYOLU-TEFSIR:36:69/r2.author: Hayreddin Karaman, Mustafa Çağrıcı, İbrahim Kâfi Dönmez, Sadrettin Gümüş
KURANYOLU-TEFSIR:36:69/r2.speaker: author
KURANYOLU-TEFSIR:36:69/r2.claim: Polytheists who rejected Muhammad’s prophethood called him a poet, but calling the Prophet a poet in the modern artistic sense could not persuade people because the Qur’an plainly is not poetry.
KURANYOLU-TEFSIR:36:69/r2.anchor: Hz. Muhammed’in peygamber olduğunu kabul etmek istemeyen ve hakkında türlü sıfatlar uyduran müşriklerin onu şair olarak nitelemeleri de bu sebebe dayanıyordu

KURANYOLU-TEFSIR:36:69/r3.author: Hayreddin Karaman, Mustafa Çağrıcı, İbrahim Kâfi Dönmez, Sadrettin Gümüş
KURANYOLU-TEFSIR:36:69/r3.speaker: author
KURANYOLU-TEFSIR:36:69/r3.claim: The cited accusations call the Prophet a poet but do not label the Qur’an poetry; the author notes that “poetry” appears only here in the Qur’an and points to the passage on poets.
KURANYOLU-TEFSIR:36:69/r3.anchor: Kur’an için “şiir” nitelemesi yer almamakta, sadece Hz. Peygamber şair olarak nitelenmekteydi

KURANYOLU-TEFSIR:36:69/r4.author: Hayreddin Karaman, Mustafa Çağrıcı, İbrahim Kâfi Dönmez, Sadrettin Gümüş
KURANYOLU-TEFSIR:36:69/r4.speaker: author
KURANYOLU-TEFSIR:36:69/r4.claim: In pre-Islamic Arab belief, a jinn could temporarily possess an ecstatic person and speak stirring words, often in verse, through him; this possession idea was widespread and later called shamanism.
KURANYOLU-TEFSIR:36:69/r4.anchor: bu varlık (bir cin) vecd halindeki bir kişiye (şair) geçici olarak sahip olur, onun ağzından çoğunlukla beyitler şeklinde, normal haldeki insanın söyleyemeyeceği heyecan veren kelimeler söylerdi

KURANYOLU-TEFSIR:36:69/r5.author: Hayreddin Karaman, Mustafa Çağrıcı, İbrahim Kâfi Dönmez, Sadrettin Gümüş
KURANYOLU-TEFSIR:36:69/r5.speaker: author
KURANYOLU-TEFSIR:36:69/r5.claim: Most surviving pre-Islamic poetry is from the late Jahiliyya, long after the primitive shamanic period; poetry had become a high art, so poets cannot all be said to have been viewed as jinn-possessed, although that remained the word’s first cultural association.
KURANYOLU-TEFSIR:36:69/r5.anchor: bize kadar gelen İslâm öncesi şiirlerin çoğunluğu, son Câhiliye devrine yani Arap şiirinin ilkel Şamanizm devrinden çok sonraya aittir

KURANYOLU-TEFSIR:36:69/r6.author: Hayreddin Karaman, Mustafa Çağrıcı, İbrahim Kâfi Dönmez, Sadrettin Gümüş
KURANYOLU-TEFSIR:36:69/r6.speaker: author
KURANYOLU-TEFSIR:36:69/r6.claim: The social standing of poets in the last pre-Islamic period was lower than it had been in earlier Arabia.
KURANYOLU-TEFSIR:36:69/r6.anchor: son Câhiliye döneminde şairin sosyal mevkiinin Arabistan’ın eski devirlerindeki gibi yüksek olmadığı da göz ardı edilmemelidir

KURANYOLU-TEFSIR:36:69/r7.author: Hayreddin Karaman, Mustafa Çağrıcı, İbrahim Kâfi Dönmez, Sadrettin Gümüş
KURANYOLU-TEFSIR:36:69/r7.speaker: author
KURANYOLU-TEFSIR:36:69/r7.claim: Many exegetes and Qur’anic-science scholars refute the allegation by assuming it calls the Qur’an poetry in the familiar artistic sense.
KURANYOLU-TEFSIR:36:69/r7.anchor: Müfessirler ve i‘câzü’l-Kur’ân gibi Kur’an ilimleriyle meşgul olanlar genellikle, burada Kur’an için, bilinen anlamıyla şiir nitelemesi yapıldığı düşüncesinden hareketle

KURANYOLU-TEFSIR:36:69/r8.author: Hayreddin Karaman, Mustafa Çağrıcı, İbrahim Kâfi Dönmez, Sadrettin Gümüş
KURANYOLU-TEFSIR:36:69/r8.speaker: Râzî
KURANYOLU-TEFSIR:36:69/r8.claim: Rāzī explains that the Qur’an answers the poet accusation in this way because the Prophet challenged his opponents only to produce something like the Qur’an, despite their also calling him a sorcerer and soothsayer.
KURANYOLU-TEFSIR:36:69/r8.anchor: Râzî, müşriklerin Hz. Peygamber’i sihirbaz ve kâhin olarak da itham etmelerine rağmen Kur’an’da ona sihir ve kehanetin öğretilmediğine dair bir ifade kullanılmayıp

KURANYOLU-TEFSIR:36:69/r9.author: Hayreddin Karaman, Mustafa Çağrıcı, İbrahim Kâfi Dönmez, Sadrettin Gümüş
KURANYOLU-TEFSIR:36:69/r9.speaker: author
KURANYOLU-TEFSIR:36:69/r9.claim: The verse clarifies the nature of the Qur’an sworn by at the sūra’s beginning and the mission assigned to Muhammad as the true Prophet.
KURANYOLU-TEFSIR:36:69/r9.anchor: sûrenin başında kendisi üzerine yemin edilen Kur’an’ın ve hak peygamber olduğu vurgulanan Hz. Muhammed’e verilen görevin mahiyetini aydınlığa kavuşturmaktır

KURANYOLU-TEFSIR:36:69/r10.author: Hayreddin Karaman, Mustafa Çağrıcı, İbrahim Kâfi Dönmez, Sadrettin Gümüş
KURANYOLU-TEFSIR:36:69/r10.speaker: author
KURANYOLU-TEFSIR:36:69/r10.claim: By observing Muhammad’s characteristics, his audience should recognize that he was not taught poetry, that poetry does not befit him, and that he is a true prophet bearing divine revelation.
KURANYOLU-TEFSIR:36:69/r10.anchor: onun şiir öğretilmiş bir kişi olmadığını, zaten bunun ona yaraşmayacağını ve ilâhî mesajı getiren gerçek bir peygamber olduğunu anlayacaklardır

KURANYOLU-TEFSIR:36:69/r11.author: Hayreddin Karaman, Mustafa Çağrıcı, İbrahim Kâfi Dönmez, Sadrettin Gümüş
KURANYOLU-TEFSIR:36:69/r11.speaker: author
KURANYOLU-TEFSIR:36:69/r11.claim: The revelation is solely an admonition, not a means for the Prophet’s personal gain, and its explanations serve humanity’s good and salvation.
KURANYOLU-TEFSIR:36:69/r11.anchor: kendisi için bir menfaat sağlama aracı olmayıp sadece insanlığın hayrına ve kurtuluşuna vesile olacak açıklamalar içermektedir

KURANYOLU-TEFSIR:36:69/r12.author: Hayreddin Karaman, Mustafa Çağrıcı, İbrahim Kâfi Dönmez, Sadrettin Gümüş
KURANYOLU-TEFSIR:36:69/r12.speaker: author
KURANYOLU-TEFSIR:36:69/r12.claim: The revelation is not mysterious knowledge or riddling speech that dulls minds; its clear content and style prompt people to think.
KURANYOLU-TEFSIR:36:69/r12.anchor: O, insanların beyinlerini uyuşturacak esrarengiz bilgiler ve bilmece gibi ifadeler taşıyan bir kelâm değildir; aksine muhteva ve üslubuyla insanı düşünmeye sevkeden apaçık bir Kur’an’dır

KURANYOLU-TEFSIR:36:69/r13.author: Hayreddin Karaman, Mustafa Çağrıcı, İbrahim Kâfi Dönmez, Sadrettin Gümüş
KURANYOLU-TEFSIR:36:69/r13.speaker: author
KURANYOLU-TEFSIR:36:69/r13.claim: The Qur’an is a divine book recited in some acts of worship, with reward for reciting it and acting according to it.
KURANYOLU-TEFSIR:36:69/r13.anchor: bazı ibadetlerde okunan ve okunup gereğince amel edilmesi karşılığında ecir alınan ilâhî bir kitaptır

BAQILLANI:v1p51/r1.author: al-Bāqillānī
BAQILLANI:v1p51/r1.speaker: author
BAQILLANI:v1p51/r1.claim: Bāqillānī begins from God’s denial that the Qur’an and Prophet are poets, alongside the condemnation of poets and the denial that the revelation is a poet’s speech.
BAQILLANI:v1p51/r1.anchor: قد علمنا أن الله تعالى نفى الشعر عن القرآن وعن النبي فقال

BAQILLANI:v1p51/r2.author: al-Bāqillānī
BAQILLANI:v1p51/r2.speaker: author
BAQILLANI:v1p51/r2.claim: He says accusations that Muhammad was a poet need not mean that the Qur’an uses familiar metrical forms; they may refer to his uniquely subtle craft in composing speech.
BAQILLANI:v1p51/r2.anchor: نسبوه إلى أنه يشعر بما لا يشعر به غيره من الصنعة اللطيفة في نظم الكلام

BAQILLANI:v1p51/r3.author: al-Bāqillānī
BAQILLANI:v1p51/r3.speaker: author
BAQILLANI:v1p51/r3.claim: Alternatively, philosophers called their sages and perceptive thinkers poets for subtle insight into speech and logic, though this is not Arabic poetry in its technical sense.
BAQILLANI:v1p51/r3.anchor: أو يكون محمولا على ما كان يطلق الفلاسفة على حكمائهم وأهل الفطنة منهم

BAQILLANI:v1p51/r4.author: al-Bāqillānī
BAQILLANI:v1p51/r4.speaker: author
BAQILLANI:v1p51/r4.claim: He considers the literal accusation by some people ignorant of poetic meters the least plausible explanation.

BAQILLANI:v1p51/r5.author: al-Bāqillānī
BAQILLANI:v1p51/r5.speaker: author
BAQILLANI:v1p51/r5.claim: The first two usages make their label intelligible: a poet notices what others miss, and one thought capable of poetry would be considered even more capable of lesser speechcraft.
BAQILLANI:v1p51/r5.anchor: فإن حمل على الوجهين الأولين كان ما أطلقوه صحيحا وذلك أن الشاعر يفطن لما لا يفطن له غيره

BURHAN:v3p35/r1.author: al-Zarkashī
BURHAN:v3p35/r1.speaker: author
BURHAN:v3p35/r1.claim: Form II can rarely indicate abundance with intransitive verbs, but in settings where abundance is impossible it does not carry that force.
BURHAN:v3p35/r1.anchor: وقد جاء التضعيف دالا على الكثرة في اللازم قليلا نحو موت المال وجاء حيث لا يمكن فيه التكثير

BURHAN:v3p35/r4.author: al-Zarkashī
BURHAN:v3p35/r4.speaker: author
BURHAN:v3p35/r4.claim: ترتيلا conveys abundant reading in a measured, reflective manner, whereas وما علمناه الشعر denies the basic act of teaching poetry rather than intensifying its negation.
BURHAN:v3p35/r4.anchor: يدل على كثرة القراءة على هيئة التأني والتدبر

JURJANI-DALAIL:v1p39/r1.author: ʿAbd al-Qāhir al-Jurjānī
JURJANI-DALAIL:v1p39/r1.speaker: author
JURJANI-DALAIL:v1p39/r1.claim: It is mistaken to treat meter and rhyme as defects that lower speech merely because it is poetry.
JURJANI-DALAIL:v1p39/r1.anchor: وإن زعم أنه ذم الشعر من حيث هو موزون مقفى ، حتى كأن الوزن عيب

JURJANI-DALAIL:v1p39/r2.author: ʿAbd al-Qāhir al-Jurjānī
JURJANI-DALAIL:v1p39/r2.speaker: العلماء
JURJANI-DALAIL:v1p39/r2.claim: The scholars say poetry is speech whose good is good and whose bad is bad; Jurjani notes that this maxim is also reported as a Prophetic marfuʿ report, without stating a grading.
JURJANI-DALAIL:v1p39/r2.anchor: العلماء في قولهم : ' إنما الشعر كلام حسنه حسن وقبيحه قبيح ' ، وقد روي ذلك عن النبي مرفوعا أيضا

JURJANI-DALAIL:v1p39/r3.author: ʿAbd al-Qāhir al-Jurjānī
JURJANI-DALAIL:v1p39/r3.speaker: author
JURJANI-DALAIL:v1p39/r3.claim: Even if meter can lead to singing and amusement, his advocacy of poetry concerns forceful diction, clear speech, apt representation, metaphor, allusion, and elevating or clarifying meaning.
JURJANI-DALAIL:v1p39/r3.anchor: فإنا إذا كنا لم ندعه إلى الشعر من أجل ذلك ، وإنما دعوناه إلى اللفظ الجزل

JURJANI-DALAIL:v1p39/r4.author: ʿAbd al-Qāhir al-Jurjānī
JURJANI-DALAIL:v1p39/r4.speaker: author
JURJANI-DALAIL:v1p39/r4.claim: The verse cannot prohibit poetry for its eloquence, since that would mean God denied the Prophet البيان والبلاغة despite the scholars' agreement that he was the most eloquent Arab.
JURJANI-DALAIL:v1p39/r4.anchor: وهذا هو الجواب لمتعلق إن تعلق بقوله تعالى : ( ﴿ وما علمناه الشعر وما ينبغي له ﴾ )

JURJANI-DALAIL:v1p39/r5.author: ʿAbd al-Qāhir al-Jurjānī
JURJANI-DALAIL:v1p39/r5.speaker: author
JURJANI-DALAIL:v1p39/r5.claim: If meter itself made speech blameworthy, blame should attach especially to its composer or seeker, not to someone reciting it for a different purpose; poetry cannot be disentangled from speech when recited.
JURJANI-DALAIL:v1p39/r5.anchor: لكان من حق العيب فيه أن يكون على واضع الشعر أو من يريده لمكان الوزن

NAHHAS:v3p404/r1.author: Abū Jaʿfar al-Naḥḥās
NAHHAS:v3p404/r1.speaker: author
NAHHAS:v3p404/r1.claim: Some scholars argue that the case endings in أنا النبي لا كذب / أنا ابن عبد المطلب disrupt poetic meter; others deny that meter is poetry, which al-Nahhas calls denial of the observable, since Khalil and others transmitted such verse.
NAHHAS:v3p404/r1.anchor: إنما الرواية بالاعراب فإن كانت بالاعراب لم تكن شعرا لأنه إذا فتح الباء من البيت الأول

NAHHAS:v3p404/r2.author: Abū Jaʿfar al-Naḥḥās
NAHHAS:v3p404/r2.speaker: أبو إسحاق
NAHHAS:v3p404/r2.claim: Abu Ishaq reads the verse as saying God did not make Muhammad a poet, which does not prevent him from reciting poetry.
NAHHAS:v3p404/r2.anchor: إن معنى وما علمناه الشعر أي وما علمناه أن يشعر أي ما جعلناه شاعرا

NAHHAS:v3p404/r3.author: Abū Jaʿfar al-Naḥḥās
NAHHAS:v3p404/r3.speaker: author
NAHHAS:v3p404/r3.claim: The verse says God did not teach Muhammad poetry, not that he never recited a poem; this is the apparent wording.
NAHHAS:v3p404/r3.anchor: وقد قيل إنما خبر الله عز وجل ما علمه الشعر ولم يخبر أنه لا ينشد شعرا وهذا ظاهر الكلام

NAHHAS:v3p404/r4.author: Abū Jaʿfar al-Naḥḥās
NAHHAS:v3p404/r4.speaker: author
NAHHAS:v3p404/r4.claim: Another linguistic view says metered speech not intended as poetry is not poetry, but only happens to match meter.
NAHHAS:v3p404/r4.anchor: كل من قال قولا موزونا لا يقصد به إلى شعر فليس بشعر وإنما وافق الشعر

NAHHAS:v3p404/r5.author: Abū Jaʿfar al-Naḥḥās
NAHHAS:v3p404/r5.speaker: أبو إسحاق
NAHHAS:v3p404/r5.claim: Abu Ishaq explains وما ينبغي له as وما يتسهل له, referring to composing poetry rather than reciting it.
NAHHAS:v3p404/r5.anchor: قال أبو إسحاق أي وما يتسهل له وتأويله على معنى وما يتسهل قول الشعر لا الإنشاد

QUSHAYRI:v3p82/r5.author: al-Qushayrī
QUSHAYRI:v3p82/r5.speaker: author
QUSHAYRI:v3p82/r5.claim: The Prophet’s speech was outside poetic meters, and the Qur’an was neither poetry nor a method of oratory; opponents were baffled because their sight lacked the light of tawhid and could not witness realities.
QUSHAYRI:v3p82/r5.anchor: والذي أتاهم به من القرآن لم يكن من أنواع الشعر ، ولا من طرق الخطباء

BURHAN:v4p104/r2.author: al-Zarkashī
BURHAN:v4p104/r2.speaker: author
BURHAN:v4p104/r2.claim: The rhetoricians say no conjunction is needed when a following clause is so closely joined that it restates or emphasizes the first, as predicate, explanation or equivalent meaning.
BURHAN:v4p104/r2.anchor: وقال البيانيون للجملة ثلاثة أحوال فالاول إن يكون ما قبلها بمنزلة الصفة من الموصوف والتاكيد من المؤكد فلا يدخلها عطف

JURJANI-DALAIL:v1p179/r1.author: ʿAbd al-Qāhir al-Jurjānī
JURJANI-DALAIL:v1p179/r1.speaker: author
JURJANI-DALAIL:v1p179/r1.claim: The positive exclusive clauses ‘it is only a reminder and clear Qurʾān’ and ‘it is only revelation’ reinforce the preceding denials that the Prophet was taught poetry or speaks from whim.
JURJANI-DALAIL:v1p179/r1.anchor: فإثبات ما علمه النبي وأوحي إليه ذكرا وقرآنا تأكيد وتثبيت لنفي أن يكون قد علم الشعر

ISLAHI-TADABBUR:vol-6-2:p409/r1.author: Amin Ahsan Islahi (d. 1997)
ISLAHI-TADABBUR:vol-6-2:p409/r1.speaker: author
ISLAHI-TADABBUR:vol-6-2:p409/r1.claim: After explaining who will benefit from the Book, the closing passage points to providential signs that call for gratitude, then reassures the Prophet to entrust opponents’ mockery to God.
ISLAHI-TADABBUR:vol-6-2:p409/r1.anchor: some very prominent signs of God’s providence are alluded to in order to once again invite people to show gratitude to God

ISLAHI-TADABBUR:vol-6-2:p410/r1.author: Amin Ahsan Islahi (d. 1997)
ISLAHI-TADABBUR:vol-6-2:p410/r1.speaker: author
ISLAHI-TADABBUR:vol-6-2:p410/r1.claim: The accusative pronoun in “We have not taught him” refers to the Prophet Muhammad.
ISLAHI-TADABBUR:vol-6-2:p410/r1.anchor: The antecedent of the accusative pronoun in ُہاَنْمَّلَع is the Prophet (sws).

ISLAHI-TADABBUR:vol-6-2:p410/r2.author: Amin Ahsan Islahi (d. 1997)
ISLAHI-TADABBUR:vol-6-2:p410/r2.speaker: author
ISLAHI-TADABBUR:vol-6-2:p410/r2.claim: The statement refutes those who called the Qur’an poetry and Muhammad a poet, using that claim to explain away its eloquence and divert people from its divine authority.
ISLAHI-TADABBUR:vol-6-2:p410/r2.anchor: This is actually a refutation of people who regard the Qur’ān to be poetry and the Prophet (sws) to be a poet.

ISLAHI-TADABBUR:vol-6-2:p410/r3.author: Amin Ahsan Islahi (d. 1997)
ISLAHI-TADABBUR:vol-6-2:p410/r3.speaker: author
ISLAHI-TADABBUR:vol-6-2:p410/r3.claim: “It is not befitting for him” means poetry is lower in status than prophethood; Islahi develops this through the different character and scope of poets’ and prophets’ work.
ISLAHI-TADABBUR:vol-6-2:p410/r3.anchor: The expression اَمَو يِغَنبَی ُهَل means that poetry is something of lesser in status to a prophet.

ISLAHI-TADABBUR:vol-6-2:p411/r1.author: Amin Ahsan Islahi (d. 1997)
ISLAHI-TADABBUR:vol-6-2:p411/r1.speaker: author
ISLAHI-TADABBUR:vol-6-2:p411/r1.claim: Poets make grand claims without practicing them, whereas prophets most fully practice what they preach.
ISLAHI-TADABBUR:vol-6-2:p411/r1.anchor: not practice what they preach. On the contrary, a prophet practices the most

ISLAHI-TADABBUR:vol-6-2:p411/r2.author: Amin Ahsan Islahi (d. 1997)
ISLAHI-TADABBUR:vol-6-2:p411/r2.speaker: author
ISLAHI-TADABBUR:vol-6-2:p411/r2.claim: Poets wander among contradictory ideas, unlike prophets, whose principles and corollaries cohere and whose speech has sequence and correspondence.
ISLAHI-TADABBUR:vol-6-2:p411/r2.anchor: Their second characteristic is that their compositions are a collection of contradictory thoughts; he wanders in every field

ISLAHI-TADABBUR:vol-6-2:p411/r3.author: Amin Ahsan Islahi (d. 1997)
ISLAHI-TADABBUR:vol-6-2:p411/r3.speaker: author
ISLAHI-TADABBUR:vol-6-2:p411/r3.claim: Strayed people follow poets, whereas God’s prophets are followed by noble and pious people.
ISLAHI-TADABBUR:vol-6-2:p411/r3.anchor: Their third characteristic is that only people who have strayed away from the truth follow poets.

ISLAHI-TADABBUR:vol-6-2:p411/r4.author: Amin Ahsan Islahi (d. 1997)
ISLAHI-TADABBUR:vol-6-2:p411/r4.speaker: author
ISLAHI-TADABBUR:vol-6-2:p411/r4.claim: The Qur’anic rule about poets has rare exceptions; God has protected His prophets from poetry’s harmful influence.
ISLAHI-TADABBUR:vol-6-2:p411/r4.anchor: For this reason, the Almighty has protected his prophets from the evil touch of poetry.

ISLAHI-TADABBUR:vol-6-2:p411/r5.author: Amin Ahsan Islahi (d. 1997)
ISLAHI-TADABBUR:vol-6-2:p411/r5.speaker: author
ISLAHI-TADABBUR:vol-6-2:p411/r5.claim: Poetry arises from and affects emotions, while prophethood addresses every sphere through intellect, moral correction, life principles and statecraft; such guidance requires a clear divine book.
ISLAHI-TADABBUR:vol-6-2:p411/r5.anchor: all poetry relates to emotions: it arises from emotions and also effects emotions.

ISLAHI-TADABBUR:vol-6-2:p411/r6.author: Amin Ahsan Islahi (d. 1997)
ISLAHI-TADABBUR:vol-6-2:p411/r6.speaker: author
ISLAHI-TADABBUR:vol-6-2:p411/r6.claim: David’s Psalms supplement the Torah with prayers, sermons and wise counsel; they are a blessed treasury with the Torah but cannot alone fulfill a messenger’s guidance mission.
ISLAHI-TADABBUR:vol-6-2:p411/r6.anchor: The status of the Psalms is that of an addendum to the Torah

ISLAHI-TADABBUR:vol-6-2:p412/r1.author: Amin Ahsan Islahi (d. 1997)
ISLAHI-TADABBUR:vol-6-2:p412/r1.speaker: author
ISLAHI-TADABBUR:vol-6-2:p412/r1.claim: As a reminder, the Qur’an recalls innate truths, the history of divine guidance from Adam to Muhammad, and the worldly and otherworldly consequences of rejecting messengers.
ISLAHI-TADABBUR:vol-6-2:p412/r1.anchor: It reminds people of the facts innately found in human nature; it also reminds people of the history of divine guidance

ISLAHI-TADABBUR:vol-6-2:p412/r2.author: Amin Ahsan Islahi (d. 1997)
ISLAHI-TADABBUR:vol-6-2:p412/r2.speaker: author
ISLAHI-TADABBUR:vol-6-2:p412/r2.claim: “Clear Qur’an” describes a comprehensive guide with unambiguous, reasoned counsel for every part of life, whose clarity leaves a fair-minded person with no doubt.
ISLAHI-TADABBUR:vol-6-2:p412/r2.anchor: It explains every fact so clearly that no doubt remains in the mind of a fair person.

ISLAHI-TADABBUR:vol-6-2:p414/r5.author: Amin Ahsan Islahi (d. 1997)
ISLAHI-TADABBUR:vol-6-2:p414/r5.speaker: author
ISLAHI-TADABBUR:vol-6-2:p414/r5.claim: The blessings and the Qur’an convey the same clear message, yet people evade it by dismissing the Qur’an as poetry instead of understanding and believing it.
ISLAHI-TADABBUR:vol-6-2:p414/r5.anchor: why are people trying to evade the Qur’ān by regarding it to be poetry instead of understanding and believing in such a clear fact.

JISHUMI:v8p5899/r1.author: al-Ḥākim al-Jishumī
JISHUMI:v8p5899/r1.speaker: عائشة
JISHUMI:v8p5899/r1.claim: Aisha says poetry was the Prophet’s most disliked speech; when he quoted a line, he reversed its beginning and end.
JISHUMI:v8p5899/r1.anchor: وسئلت عائشة: أكان النبي - صلى الله عليه وسلم - يتمثل بالشعر؟ قالت: كان أبغض الحديث إليه الشعر

JISHUMI:v8p5899/r2.author: al-Ḥākim al-Jishumī
JISHUMI:v8p5899/r2.speaker: عائشة
JISHUMI:v8p5899/r2.claim: Aisha reports that when the Prophet intended to quote a line, he put its end first.
JISHUMI:v8p5899/r2.anchor: غير أنه كان إذا أراد أن يتمثل ببيت جعل أوله آخره

JISHUMI:v8p5899/r3.author: al-Ḥākim al-Jishumī
JISHUMI:v8p5899/r3.speaker: author
JISHUMI:v8p5899/r3.claim: Jishumi offers either that the Prophet did not attend to memorizing poetry or that God diverted him from it.
JISHUMI:v8p5899/r3.anchor: قلنا: يحتمل أنه لم يصرف عنايته إلى حفظ شيء منه، ويحتمل أنه تعالى صرفه عن ذلك

JISHUMI:v8p5899/r4.author: al-Ḥākim al-Jishumī
JISHUMI:v8p5899/r4.speaker: القاضي
JISHUMI:v8p5899/r4.claim: Al-Qadi reads the verse as denying that the Prophet composed poetry, while finding it unlikely that he could not memorize others’ poems.
JISHUMI:v8p5899/r4.anchor: قال القاضي: والآية محمولة على أنه لا ينشئ، وأما حفظ شعر غيره فيبعد ألا يحفظه

JISHUMI:v8p5899/r5.author: al-Ḥākim al-Jishumī
JISHUMI:v8p5899/r5.speaker: القاضي
JISHUMI:v8p5899/r5.claim: Al-Qadi explains the reversal of a line’s order as showing that otherwise it would have been poetry.
JISHUMI:v8p5899/r5.anchor: قال: وإنما كان يجعل أوله آخره لعلمه أنه لولاه لكان شعرا

JISHUMI:v8p5899/r6.author: al-Ḥākim al-Jishumī
JISHUMI:v8p5899/r6.speaker: author
JISHUMI:v8p5899/r6.claim: The discussion cites transmitted prophetic phrases, including Ana al-nabiyyu la kadhib, while considering the claim that he did not compose poetry.
JISHUMI:v8p5899/r6.anchor: وما يروى من قوله: أنا النبي لا كذب، وقوله: هل أنت

BURHAN:v2p111/r6.author: al-Zarkashī
BURHAN:v2p111/r6.speaker: author
BURHAN:v2p111/r6.claim: The Qur’an is purified of poetic meter because it is truth and a source of truth, unlike poetry’s tendency to portray falsehood as truth and exaggerate praise or blame.
BURHAN:v2p111/r6.anchor: فأعلم سبحانه أنه نزة الفرآن عن نظم الشعر والوزن لأن القرآ مجمع الحق ومنبع الصدق وقصارى أمر الشاعر التحصل بتصوير الباطل فى صورة الحق
